title: Build the lifecycle program in revenue order, not by whim
hypothesis: If we build deliverability and tracking first, then cart and checkout flows, then welcome, then popup, then post-purchase, then segments, then campaigns, then win-back and sunset, then SMS, then copy and design tests, then loyalty extras, in that order, then email and SMS revenue grows faster because effort goes to the highest-revenue-per-hour work first instead of the newest idea.

signal.check: The brand has no written build order, or is working on low-priority items (button colours, loyalty extras) while core flows like cart or welcome are missing or weak.

risk.note: Planning only; reorders work, does not change anything live.

prerequisites: A list of every flow, segment and campaign currently live or missing
steps: List every flow, popup, segment and campaign the brand has and does not have.
Mark deliverability, tracking and attribution as done or not done.
Rank the gaps: cart and checkout, welcome, popup, post-purchase, segments, campaigns, win-back and sunset, SMS, testing, loyalty extras.
Pick the top 1 to 2 gaps and schedule them before any lower-priority work.

test.method: Not a test in itself; re-check the plan matches actual build order after each 30-day cycle.

title: Fix the 3 basics before any advanced email work
hypothesis: If we check the popup opt-in rate, the presence of a real cart flow, and welcome flow length before starting cross-sell splits or hyper-segmentation, then revenue moves faster because the biggest gaps get fixed first instead of layering complexity on a weak base.

signal.check: Popup opt-in rate is below 3 percent, or there is no flow triggered on Added to Cart with 6 or more emails, or the welcome flow has only 1 email.

risk.note: A checklist step; no live change by itself.

prerequisites: Current popup opt-in rate
List of live flows and their email counts
steps: Check popup opt-in rate against 3 to 9 percent.
Check whether a real Added to Cart flow with 6 or more emails exists.
Check whether the welcome flow has more than 1 email.
If any check fails, fix it before building segment splits or advanced personalisation.

test.method: Not a test; a gate to run before starting new segmentation or split work.
test.read_point: Before starting any new segmentation project

title: Track the flow-to-campaign revenue split and rebalance toward half and half
hypothesis: If we measure flow revenue against campaign revenue and treat anything near 30 percent flows as a sign flows need work, then total email revenue moves up because the highest-margin automated revenue gets rebuilt instead of ignored.

signal.check: Flow revenue is a clear minority of total email revenue, for example under 35 percent, with no recent flow work.

expected_effect.size: 40 to 60 percent of email revenue from flows, either direction

risk.note: A measurement step, not a change.

prerequisites: Flow and campaign revenue reported separately for the same period
steps: Pull flow revenue and campaign revenue for the last 30 to 90 days.
Compute the flow share of the total.
If flows are near 30 percent or below, prioritise flow builds over new campaigns.
Recheck monthly.

test.method: Compare flow share before and after flow-focused work.
test.read_point: After 60 to 90 days of flow work

title: Set a 30 percent email revenue share target and track it with clean attribution
hypothesis: If we track email-attributed revenue as a share of total store revenue, with transactional emails, bot clicks and Apple opens excluded, then we get an honest read on the channel because inflated attribution stops hiding a weak program.

signal.check: Email-attributed revenue share is unknown, is measured with default attribution settings, or is well below 30 percent.

expected_effect.size: 30 percent or more of store revenue once the program is built

risk.note: Measurement change only.

prerequisites: Attribution window and exclusions set per platform (see attribution settings idea)
steps: Confirm attribution excludes transactional messages, bot clicks and Apple privacy opens.
Pull email-attributed revenue and total store revenue for the same period.
Compute the share and compare to 30 percent.
Flag the attribution window used alongside the number, since it changes the result.

test.method: Re-measure monthly after attribution is cleaned up and after flow and campaign builds.

title: Map the full customer journey before building or changing any flow
hypothesis: If we write out the path from ad or post, to popup, to welcome or abandonment flow, to campaigns, to first order, to post-purchase, to the next order, then flow and campaign mistakes drop because each touchpoint is checked against what the person already knows.

signal.check: No written map exists of what a shopper sees at each stage, and offers or messages sometimes contradict what a customer already received, such as a first-order discount sent to a 5-order customer.

risk.note: A planning document; no live change.

prerequisites: List of every touchpoint: ads, posts, popup, flows, campaigns
steps: List every touchpoint from first ad or post through to repeat order.
Write what the person already knows or has received at each stage.
Check every current flow and campaign offer against that map.
Fix any mismatch, such as an acquisition discount going to a repeat customer.

test.method: Not a test; a reference document checked before each new build.
test.measure: Number of mismatched offers found and fixed

title: Turn any weekly repeated campaign into an automated flow
hypothesis: If we convert a campaign that gets sent the same way every week into an automated flow, then team time moves to new content because flows capture demand automatically while campaigns should only create new demand.

signal.check: The same campaign, such as a weekly bestseller reminder or an evergreen education send, goes out on a fixed schedule with little change week to week.

risk.note: Can be turned back into a manual campaign if it underperforms.

prerequisites: A campaign sent on a fixed repeating schedule
steps: Identify campaigns that repeat on a fixed schedule with little change.
Pick the trigger and audience condition that would fire it automatically.
Build it as a flow instead of a manual send.
Free the manual send slot for new campaign content.

test.method: Compare revenue per recipient of the automated flow version against the old manual campaign.
test.read_point: After 4 to 6 sends of the new flow

title: Exclude people who just got a flow email from that day's campaign
hypothesis: If we exclude anyone who received a welcome, cart or post-purchase flow email in the last 24 hours from a campaign send, then unsubscribes and complaints go down because no one gets hit twice in one day by accident.

signal.check: Campaign audiences are built with no exclusion for people currently inside a high-frequency flow, and complaints or unsubscribes spike after some sends.

risk.note: Only changes who is excluded from a send.

prerequisites: Ability to add a dynamic exclusion condition at send time
steps: Identify time-critical flows: welcome, cart, checkout, post-purchase email 1.
Add a campaign exclusion for anyone who entered one of those flows in the last 24 hours.
Tick the setting that determines recipients at send time so the exclusion is live, not stale.
Check unsubscribe and complaint rate after the change.

test.method: Compare unsubscribe rate for campaigns with and without the exclusion.
test.read_point: After 3 to 4 campaign sends with the exclusion live

title: Build the popup offer first, before behaviour, copy or design changes
hypothesis: If we fix the popup's offer before touching trigger timing, copy or design, then opt-in rate moves the most because the offer is the biggest lever and small design hacks barely move a weak offer.

signal.check: The popup offer is generic, such as sign up for updates or a small percent off, and recent testing has focused on colours, delay or copy instead of the offer.

expected_effect.size: unknown, but design-only changes on a weak offer move opt-in rate by roughly 0.2 points

risk.note: Reversible copy and offer change on the form.

prerequisites: Current AOV and margin to size the offer
steps: Write out the current popup offer exactly as shown.
Compare it against AOV-based sizing (see the percent vs dollar idea).
Rewrite the offer to be a clear, sized discount or gift, not generic wording.
Only then test behaviour, copy and design in that order.

test.method: A/B test the new offer against the old one at 50/50 split.
test.measure: other:opt_in_rate and welcome flow placed order rate
test.read_point: After 3,000 to 5,000 impressions per variant or 15 days

title: Target an 8 to 12 percent popup opt-in rate, tested per device
hypothesis: If we measure and test the popup toward 8 to 12 percent of site traffic per device, then the list grows faster because most untested forms only convert 1 to 4 percent and are leaving signups behind.

signal.check: Current popup opt-in rate by device is unknown or is between 1 and 4 percent of visitors.

expected_effect.size: from 1 to 4 percent toward 8 to 12 percent of traffic

risk.note: Measurement plus iterative testing, not a single risky change.

prerequisites: Form analytics showing views and submits by device
steps: Pull current opt-in rate by device from the form analytics.
Compare to the 8 to 12 percent target.
If below target, run the leverage-order testing plan starting with the offer.
Recheck the rate after each test.

test.method: Track opt-in rate by device across each test cycle.

title: Choose percent off or dollars off based on AOV
hypothesis: If we use percent off below about 100 to 200 dollars AOV and dollars off above that, then signup and welcome conversion move because the discount reads as bigger to the shopper at the AOV it applies to.
does_not_apply_when: The brand's margin cannot support a 10 percent discount at all

signal.check: The popup uses a flat percent or flat dollar discount with no check against the brand's own AOV.

expected_effect.size: unknown, test against the current format

risk.note: Changes signup discount depth; watch margin.

prerequisites: Current AOV and gross margin
steps: Pull current AOV.
If AOV is under about 100 to 200 dollars, use a percent off offer, minimum 10 percent.
If AOV is at or above that, switch to a dollar amount, roughly 10 percent of AOV in dollars.
Test the switch rather than assuming it wins.

test.method: A/B test percent vs dollar format on the popup.

title: Judge a signup offer on 4 numbers together, not opt-in rate alone
hypothesis: If we judge a new signup offer on opt-in rate, total signups, welcome flow placed order rate and revenue, and margin together, plus site conversion rate, then we avoid launching an offer that raises signups but loses money or hurts checkout.

signal.check: A popup offer test or change is being judged only on opt-in rate, with no read on welcome flow conversion, revenue, margin or full-site conversion rate.

risk.note: An evaluation method, not a live change by itself.

prerequisites: Ability to read welcome flow placed order rate and revenue by offer variant
Site conversion rate before and after
steps: Before launching an offer test, list the 4 numbers to track: opt-in rate, total signups, welcome placed order rate and revenue, margin.
Also track full-site conversion rate before and after.
After the test period, compare all numbers together, not opt-in rate alone.
Pick the winner only if it does not lose money or drop site conversion.

test.method: Run the offer test as normal, but score it on the full set of numbers above.
test.measure: other:opt_in_rate, welcome placed order rate, cvr_overall
test.read_point: After the popup test's normal read point

title: Ask for 1 input per popup step, email before phone
hypothesis: If we split the popup into 1 field per step, collecting email first and phone on a later step, then submit rate rises because a single crowded step with multiple fields loses more people than a short sequence of easy steps.

signal.check: The popup asks for email and phone on the same screen, or asks for name, birthday or interests before email.

risk.note: Form structure change only.

prerequisites: Popup builder access
steps: Review the current popup's fields per step.
Move phone, name, birthday and interests to their own later step.
Keep only email on the first data-collecting step.
Preview on mobile to confirm 1 field per screen.

test.method: A/B test the multi-step, 1-field version against the current form.

title: Add a micro-commitment step before the email field, and test it
hypothesis: If we put a yes/no question, a 1-question quiz, or a scratch-off before the email field, then opt-in rate rises for most brands because a small early yes makes the next step feel like a continuation, not a new decision.

signal.check: The popup jumps straight to an email field with no earlier micro-commitment step, and this has never been tested.

expected_effect.size: unknown, some brands see no lift

risk.note: Adds a step to the form; can be removed if it does not test well.

prerequisites: Popup builder with multi-step support
steps: Design a micro-yes step, such as Do you want 10 percent off, with Yes please and No thanks buttons.
Set the Yes button to advance to the email step.
Set the No thanks button to close the form.
A/B test this version against the current straight-to-email form.

test.method: A/B test manual 50/50, decided on total signups and welcome flow revenue, not opt-in rate alone.
test.measure: other:opt_in_rate, total signups, welcome flow revenue
test.read_point: After 3,000 to 5,000 impressions per variant or 15 days

title: If using a gamified popup, only show prizes that can actually be won
hypothesis: If a spin-to-win or scratch-off popup only shows prizes the shopper can actually land, then trust holds and refunds or complaints stay low because no one discovers the wheel or scratch result was rigged against them.

signal.check: A gamified popup tool is live or being considered, and any prize slice or scratch result cannot actually be won.

risk.note: Fake prizes are a legal and trust risk in some markets; check local promotion rules.

prerequisites: Access to the gamified popup tool's prize configuration
steps: List every prize or outcome the tool can show.
Confirm each one can actually be delivered to a winner.
Remove or fix any decoy slice or fake scratch result.
Check local rules on promotions and decoy prizes before launch.

test.method: Not a test; a compliance and trust check before or during a gamified popup launch.
test.measure: Whether every shown prize is winnable
test.read_point: Before launch and at every prize change

title: Set the popup to trigger on a 4 to 12 second delay or scroll, never on load
hypothesis: If we trigger the popup at 4 to 12 seconds, or on 50 to 60 percent scroll, or desktop-only exit intent, with the rule logic set to any condition firing, then opt-in rate and site experience both improve because immediate popups and 30-second delays either annoy visitors or miss them entirely.
does_not_apply_when: Traffic bounces so fast that total submits are higher with an immediate popup, proven by testing

signal.check: The popup shows immediately on page load, waits 30 seconds, or uses exit intent on mobile.

risk.note: Timing setting change only.

prerequisites: Popup builder trigger settings
steps: Set a time delay of 4 to 6 seconds to start.
Add scroll depth of 50 to 60 percent as an OR condition.
Add desktop-only exit intent as an OR condition, keep it off on mobile.
Set the rule logic to any condition firing, not all conditions.

test.method: Test 4 vs 12 second delay, then immediate vs 4 seconds, judged on total submits and site conversion rate.

title: Re-show a closed popup after 3 to 5 days, never after a submit
hypothesis: If the popup re-shows 3 to 5 days after a close and never shows again after a submit, then opt-in rate holds and site experience improves because visitors are not nagged every visit.

signal.check: The popup shows on every visit regardless of a prior close or submit.

risk.note: Frequency setting only.

prerequisites: Popup builder frequency settings
steps: Set re-show after close to 3 to 5 days.
Confirm the form is set to never show again after a submit.
Confirm existing subscribers are excluded regardless of re-show timing.

test.method: Compare bounce and opt-in rate before and after the frequency fix.

title: Build separate mobile and desktop popup forms
hypothesis: If we clone the popup into a mobile version with no image, larger text and no exit intent, then mobile opt-in rate rises because the desktop layout, sized for a bigger screen, loads slower and reads worse on a phone.
does_not_apply_when: Testing shows 1 shared form converts equally on both devices

signal.check: The same popup form and image run on both mobile and desktop, with no per-device test on record.

risk.note: A clone of the existing form; original stays until the new one is confirmed.

prerequisites: Popup builder clone function
steps: Clone the current popup form.
On the mobile version, remove the image, enlarge text and buttons, and turn off exit intent.
On the desktop version, keep or test a side image.
Publish both and confirm each shows only on its target device.

test.method: Track opt-in rate by device after the split, or A/B test 1 shared form against the split for proof.

title: Make the popup form big, the copy short, and the offer the largest element
hypothesis: If the popup fills most of the screen, uses under 10 words of copy, and makes the offer the biggest visual element with a benefit-worded button, then opt-in rate rises because the shopper reads the whole offer in under 3 seconds.

signal.check: The popup is small, wordy, uses sign up or subscribe wording, or buries the offer under a greeting or sub-headline.

risk.note: Copy and layout change on the existing form.

prerequisites: Popup builder access
steps: Resize the form to about 75 percent of the screen.
Cut the headline and body copy to under 10 words.
Put the offer number in the headline as the largest text.
Change the button to a first-person benefit phrase such as Claim my discount.
Remove sign up, subscribe, or exclusive offers wording.

test.method: A/B test the redesigned form against the current one.

title: Suppress the popup for subscribers, cart and checkout pages, wholesale pages and non-ship countries
hypothesis: If we exclude existing profiles, cart, checkout and wholesale pages, and countries the brand does not ship to, then the popup stops wasting the offer and annoying people it cannot serve, and site experience improves for buyers mid-checkout.

signal.check: The popup shows to existing subscribers, on the cart or checkout page, on wholesale pages, or to visitors from countries the brand does not ship to.

risk.note: Targeting setting change only.

prerequisites: List of ship-to countries and any wholesale URLs
steps: Turn on the setting to not show to existing Klaviyo or platform profiles.
Exclude the cart, checkout and any wholesale URLs from the popup.
Set location targeting to ship-to countries only.
Confirm with a preview on each excluded page and profile type.

test.method: Not a split test; confirm exclusions hold with test visits and profiles.
test.measure: Whether the popup fires on any excluded page or profile
test.read_point: Immediately after the change, and monthly in the pop-up review

title: Turn on the popup teaser tab, sized to avoid other on-site widgets
hypothesis: If we turn on a small teaser tab after a popup close, shaped to avoid chat or loyalty widgets on mobile, then total subscriber count rises because visitors who closed the popup still have an easy way back to it.
does_not_apply_when: Testing shows opt-ins do not move and the teaser gets in the way of other widgets

signal.check: The popup teaser is off, or overlaps a chat or loyalty widget on mobile.

risk.note: Setting toggle; easy to revert.

prerequisites: Popup builder teaser settings
steps: Turn on the teaser tab in the popup settings.
Set it to a small circle or corner shape on mobile.
Check it does not overlap chat, loyalty or other on-site widgets.
Test off again if opt-ins do not move after 30 days.

test.method: Compare total subscriber count and opt-in rate before and after enabling the teaser.

title: Run a campaign send-time test using far-apart windows over several sends
hypothesis: If a campaign send-time test compares 2 far-apart windows, such as 7am vs 7pm, over 5 to 10 campaigns and narrows from there, then the brand finds its own best send time because a single send is too noisy to trust.

signal.check: Campaign send time is fixed by habit, such as always 9am, with no test ever run against a different window.

risk.note: Scheduling test only.

prerequisites: Enough campaign volume to run 5 to 10 comparable sends
steps: Set up a send-time test comparing 2 far-apart windows, such as 7am vs 7pm.
Use placed order rate as the winning metric, or click rate if placed order rate is not available at this level.
Run the test across 5 to 10 campaigns and compare average revenue.
Narrow the window on the next round, such as 7am vs 11am, then 11am vs 2pm.

test.method: Repeated send-time A/B test across multiple campaigns.
test.measure: email_click_rate and placed order rate by send-time window
test.read_point: After 5 to 10 campaigns per window pair

title: Compute expected SMS cost per campaign before sending
hypothesis: If expected SMS cost is computed in code before every campaign, recipients times segments times the per-segment rate, then SMS spend stays predictable because the cost is known before the send instead of discovered on the bill afterward.

signal.check: SMS campaigns are scheduled with no pre-send cost estimate, so total spend is only known after the bill arrives.

expected_effect.size: predictability, not necessarily a lower rate

risk.note: Pre-send calculation only.

prerequisites: Per-segment rate on the brand's SMS plan
Audience size for the send
steps: Confirm the message's segment count using the platform's counter.
Confirm the per-segment rate on the brand's current plan.
Compute expected cost in code: recipients times segments times rate.
Compare expected cost against expected revenue before sending, especially for MMS.

test.method: Not a split test; compare the pre-send cost estimate against the actual billed cost.

title: Treat AI analysis of email exports as hypotheses, not findings
hypothesis: If AI-generated observations from a campaign or flow export are checked against the raw CSV before being acted on, then wasted test cycles drop because an AI summary can misread a pattern that a direct read of the numbers reveals is not real.

signal.check: An AI tool's analysis of an email export was acted on directly, with no check against the underlying CSV.

expected_effect.size: fewer wasted tests from acting on a wrong AI read

risk.note: Verification step, not a live change.

prerequisites: Campaign and flow analytics export
steps: Export campaign and flow analytics for the chosen period.
Ask an AI tool for observations and recommendations.
Check each finding against the raw export: revenue per recipient by email, opens by day, send-time clusters.
Turn only the findings that hold up under direct inspection into an actual test.

test.method: Not a split test; a verification step before acting on any AI-generated finding.
test.measure: Share of AI findings confirmed against the raw export
test.read_point: Before turning any AI finding into a test

title: Test guarantee window length using the brand's own refund data
hypothesis: If the brand's guarantee window is tested against its own refund data rather than copied from another source, then the brand avoids a window that quietly costs more in returns than it gains in confidence, since a longer guarantee can return less than a shorter one if buyers simply forget to use it.

signal.check: The guarantee window length was chosen without checking it against the brand's own refund rate by window.

risk.note: Changing a guarantee window affects customer expectations; communicate any change clearly.

prerequisites: Refund rate by guarantee window, if the brand has tested more than 1
steps: Pull the brand's own refund rate data, broken out by how long after purchase a refund was requested.
Compare the current guarantee window against where most real refund requests actually land.
If untested, run a controlled test of 2 window lengths, keeping everything else equal.
Use the brand's real guarantee in every email, never inflate it beyond the tested or offered policy.

test.method: Compare return rate and stated satisfaction between guarantee window variants.
test.read_point: After enough orders have passed the guarantee window to read return rate, typically 60 to 90 days

title: Track SMS-attributed revenue as a share of total store revenue
hypothesis: If SMS-attributed revenue share is tracked against a 5 to 20 percent benchmark, then an underperforming SMS program gets flagged and fixed instead of running unmeasured alongside email.
does_not_apply_when: No SMS program is live

signal.check: SMS-attributed revenue share is unknown, or has never been compared to a benchmark once SMS has been live for several months.

expected_effect.size: 5 to 20 percent of store revenue once the program is built

risk.note: Measurement only.

prerequisites: SMS-attributed revenue and total store revenue for the same period
steps: Pull SMS-attributed revenue and total store revenue for the same period.
Compute the share and compare against 5 to 20 percent of store revenue.
If well below the benchmark after several months live, review cadence, content and list size.
Recheck monthly alongside the email revenue share benchmark.

test.method: Re-measure monthly after any SMS program change.

title: Send the discount code by email 1 instead of showing it on the success page
hypothesis: If we withhold the discount code from the popup success page and send it in welcome email 1, then sender reputation improves because that first email earns a real open and click instead of never being needed.
does_not_apply_when: The owner prefers instant reveal and accepts the small conversion loss

signal.check: The popup success page already shows the code, so subscribers have no reason to open welcome email 1.

expected_effect.size: small conversion loss on the popup itself, recovered within about 72 hours per source claims

risk.note: Copy change on the success page and welcome email 1.

prerequisites: Welcome flow email 1 built and able to carry the code
steps: Remove the code from the popup success page.
Write success copy: your code is on its way, check your inbox, check spam if not there in 5 minutes.
Confirm welcome email 1 shows the code above the fold.
Watch welcome email 1 open rate after the change.

test.method: Compare welcome email 1 open and click rate before and after withholding the code.

title: Compress every popup image and drop images on the mobile form
hypothesis: If we compress every popup image and remove images from the mobile form, then submit rate rises because a slow-loading popup loses people before it finishes rendering.

signal.check: Popup images are uncompressed or the mobile form still shows an image, and the popup visibly lags on mobile data.

risk.note: Image swap only.

prerequisites: Image compression tool
steps: Run every popup image through a compression tool.
Remove the image entirely from the mobile form.
Preview the popup on a throttled mobile connection.
Confirm no visible lag before the form renders.

test.method: Compare mobile opt-in rate before and after compression.

title: Run popup tests one at a time, offer first and colour last
hypothesis: If we test the popup in leverage order, offer first and colour last, one variable at a time with a manual 50/50 split and a manual winner, then each test cycle actually moves opt-in rate because effort goes to the biggest levers first.

signal.check: Recent popup tests changed colours, images or minor copy while the offer and form type have never been tested.

risk.note: Test process change; each test itself is reversible.

prerequisites: Popup A/B test tool with manual weight and manual winner selection
steps: List the leverage order: offer, form type and first step, close mechanics, delay, image, copy, colours.
Pick the highest untested lever on the list.
Set the test to manual 50/50 weight and manual winner, never automatic on low volume.
Run for 3,000 to 5,000 impressions per variant or 15 days, whichever is longer.
Decide the winner on total signups, welcome flow revenue and site conversion rate, not opt-in rate alone.
Log the result and move to the next item on the leverage list.

test.method: Manual 50/50 A/B test per variable, run monthly or more often.
test.measure: other:opt_in_rate, total signups, welcome flow revenue
test.read_point: After 3,000 to 5,000 impressions per variant or 15 days

title: Add 3 more list-growth channels beyond the popup, each with its own welcome
hypothesis: If we add a checkout opt-in checkbox, dedicated signup pages for social and giveaways, and footer or inline embeds, each feeding its own list and welcome flow, then list growth rises because the popup stops being the only source and each channel gets a matching first message.

signal.check: The popup is the only active list-growth method, and any giveaway or social import shares the same welcome flow and same 10 percent off offer as the popup.

risk.note: Adds new capture points; does not remove the existing popup.

prerequisites: Checkout platform opt-in checkbox capability
A giveaway or social signup page tool
steps: Turn on the checkout opt-in checkbox with proper consent wording.
Build a dedicated signup page for social followers or giveaway entrants.
Add footer and inline embed signup forms to key pages.
Give each import or giveaway list its own welcome flow, not the popup's 10 percent off welcome.

test.method: Track list growth by source over time.

title: Collect phone numbers from day 1, even before SMS is live
hypothesis: If we start collecting phone numbers as soon as the popup exists, even with no SMS program running yet, then a future SMS launch earns revenue faster because it starts with a list instead of zero.

signal.check: The popup collects only email, and no phone step exists even though the brand plans to run SMS later.

risk.note: Adds a phone step with proper consent; no SMS sent until the program launches.

prerequisites: SMS consent wording appropriate for the brand's market
steps: Add a phone step to the popup after the email step.
Include SMS consent wording appropriate for the market.
Store the phone numbers on a dedicated SMS list even with no sends yet.
Launch SMS later against an already-built list.

test.method: Not a test; a pre-build step measured by list size growth.

title: Exclude marketplace-channel customers from the popup and acquisition sends
hypothesis: If we exclude customers who bought through Amazon or another marketplace from the popup and first-order discount sends, then the brand avoids wasting the offer and avoids breaking marketplace terms, because these customers cannot legally or practically be emailed the same way as direct customers.

signal.check: The brand sells on a marketplace and marketplace-channel customer emails, where held, are still shown the signup popup or a first-order discount.

risk.note: Not excluding these customers can break marketplace terms; verify against brand data before use.

prerequisites: List of marketplace channels sold on
Whether the brand holds any customer email from that channel
steps: List every marketplace the brand sells through.
Identify whether the brand holds customer emails from any of them.
Exclude those customers from the popup and acquisition discount sends the same way as wholesale.
Check marketplace terms before emailing any customer acquired there.

test.method: Not a split test; a compliance check.
test.measure: Whether marketplace customers are excluded from acquisition sends

title: Decide single vs double opt-in for email by market law, and back single opt-in with engaged segments
hypothesis: If we default to single opt-in where the market allows it, backed by engaged segments and a sunset flow, and use double opt-in only where required, then list growth stays high while list quality is still managed, because double opt-in can massively cut subscribers where it is not required.
does_not_apply_when: The recipient's market requires double opt-in by law

signal.check: The account uses double opt-in with no legal requirement for it, or uses single opt-in with no engaged segments or sunset flow to manage quality.

expected_effect.size: unknown, double opt-in described as massively cutting subscribers where not required

risk.note: Requires a web check on consent law per market before switching.

prerequisites: Engaged segments and a sunset flow live (see segment ideas)
Web check on opt-in law per market
steps: Check opt-in law for each market the brand sends to.
Default to single opt-in for email where allowed.
Confirm engaged segments and a sunset flow are live before relying on single opt-in.
Use double opt-in only where the market requires it or the platform expects it.

test.method: Not a split test; a policy decision checked against list growth and engagement quality.
test.read_point: After the policy is set and 60 days of new signups

title: Keep consent text legible on every form in every market
hypothesis: If we keep the consent text legible size and present on every form step, in every market, then the brand avoids the deceptive-consent risk that comes from shrinking it to an unreadable size or deleting it.

signal.check: Consent text has been shrunk to a tiny font, deleted for a US-only store, or is otherwise hard to read on any form step.

expected_effect.size: unknown, legible consent text costs little to no conversion

risk.note: Text size and presence fix on existing forms.

prerequisites: Access to every live form
steps: Review every popup, checkout and signup page's consent text size.
Restore any deleted consent text.
Increase any shrunk consent text to a legible size on both mobile and desktop.
Recheck after any form redesign.

test.method: Not a split test; a compliance and trust check.
test.measure: Whether consent text is legible on every form
test.read_point: Before and after every form redesign

title: Collect explicit SMS consent separate from email consent
hypothesis: If SMS consent is always collected as its own explicit step, separate from email consent, then the SMS program avoids sending to people who never agreed to texts, because a checkout email checkbox may not count as SMS consent in every market.

signal.check: Anyone on the SMS list opted in only through an email checkbox, or SMS consent was not collected as its own explicit step.

risk.note: Texting without valid consent is a legal risk in most markets; check consent records before any SMS send.

prerequisites: Web check on SMS consent wording and separate checkbox rules per country
steps: Audit the SMS list for anyone without a separate, explicit SMS opt-in record.
Remove or re-permission anyone without valid consent.
Add a dedicated SMS consent step with required disclosures.
Check country-specific SMS consent rules before sending in a new market.

test.method: Not a split test; a compliance audit before any SMS send.
test.measure: Share of SMS list with explicit, separate consent on record
test.read_point: Before launching or expanding SMS to a new market

title: Add a subscribed-because-of-consent condition to EU segments
hypothesis: If EU segments add a because person subscribed condition, or keep 2 segment versions, then marketing sends stay compliant because someone can be emailable through a checkout entry without having given marketing consent.

signal.check: The brand sends to EU customers and segment logic does not separate marketing consent from general emailability.

risk.note: Web check GDPR consent rules for the brand's EU markets before finalising.

prerequisites: Web check on GDPR consent rules for the brand's markets
steps: Identify every segment used for EU marketing sends.
Add a condition requiring marketing consent, not just general emailability.
Alternatively, keep 2 segment versions, 1 for EU and 1 for elsewhere.
Confirm with a web check on current GDPR consent rules.

test.method: Not a split test; a compliance check on EU segment logic.
test.measure: Whether EU segments require marketing consent, not just emailability

title: Make unsubscribing 1-click and honour it immediately
hypothesis: If unsubscribing is 1-click and processed at once, then win-back, sunset and revenue-per-recipient numbers become trustworthy because a subscriber who cannot leave keeps sitting inside those counts and skewing them.

signal.check: Unsubscribing takes more than 1 click, or there is a delay before it takes effect.

risk.note: A compliance and trust fix; check the Gmail one-click unsubscribe requirement.

prerequisites: Web check on Gmail and Yahoo one-click unsubscribe requirement
steps: Test the unsubscribe flow from a real email.
Confirm it takes 1 click and applies immediately.
Add a thank-you line on the unsubscribe confirmation page.
Recheck after any template or platform change.

test.method: Not a split test; a functional check on the unsubscribe path.
test.measure: Number of clicks and time to effect for unsubscribing
test.read_point: After any email platform or template change

title: Give every flow a trigger, entry filter, exit filter and re-entry rule
hypothesis: If every flow has a trigger, entry filters, exit filters checked before every email, and a re-entry rule, then customers stop getting irrelevant emails because a buyer between email 1 and 2 is filtered out instead of receiving email 2 anyway.

signal.check: Any live flow is missing an exit filter, so a person who already converted or moved stages keeps receiving the rest of the sequence.

risk.note: Filter additions only; no content change.

prerequisites: Access to every live flow's settings
steps: Open each live flow and check for a defined trigger, entry filter, exit filter and re-entry rule.
Add exit filters using since starting this flow logic where a stage-exit event applies, such as placed order or checkout started.
Add a re-entry rule appropriate to the flow's cycle.
Preview with a test profile that would trigger the exit filter.

test.method: Not a split test; a completeness audit run per flow.
test.measure: Number of flows with all 4 elements present

title: Add exit filters so no 2 flows run for the same person at the same stage
hypothesis: If cart flow filters out checkout starters, browse flow filters out cart adders, and site flow filters out product viewers, then customers stop receiving 2 conflicting recovery emails at once, which keeps the messaging coherent.

signal.check: A test profile that moves from browsing to cart to checkout can be found inside more than 1 abandonment flow at once.

risk.note: Filter additions only.

prerequisites: Site abandonment, browse, cart and checkout flows built
steps: Add checkout started 0 as an exit filter on the cart flow.
Add added to cart 0 as an exit filter on the browse flow.
Add viewed product 0 as an exit filter on the site abandonment flow.
Test with a profile that moves through all 3 stages and confirm only 1 flow fires at a time.

test.method: Not a split test; a functional audit with a test profile moving through each stage.
test.measure: Number of flows a single test profile enters at once

title: Turn smart sending off on time-critical flow emails, on for campaigns
hypothesis: If smart sending is off on welcome, browse, cart, checkout and post-purchase email 1, and on for campaigns and later low-urgency flow emails, then recovery revenue rises because a campaign in the last 16 hours no longer blocks a time-critical cart or checkout email.

signal.check: Smart sending is on for cart, checkout, browse, welcome or post-purchase email 1, or off for campaigns.

risk.note: Watch unsubscribes per person-week since total send pressure can rise; see the monthly review.

prerequisites: List of every flow email's current smart sending state
steps: List every flow email and its current smart sending setting.
Turn smart sending off on welcome, browse, cart, checkout and post-purchase email 1.
Turn smart sending on for late post-purchase, win-back and sunset emails, and for all campaigns.
Watch unsubscribe rate per person-week in the monthly review.

test.method: Compare recovery flow revenue before and after the smart sending fix.
test.measure: other:revenue_per_recipient on cart and checkout flows

title: Turn UTM tracking on for every flow and campaign email
hypothesis: If UTM tracking is on for every flow and campaign email, then flow and campaign revenue splits cleanly from paid and organic in the analytics platform, which is the split that decides the flow-versus-campaign revenue target.

signal.check: Any flow or campaign email has UTM tracking turned off, so its revenue cannot be split cleanly from other channels.

expected_effect.size: measurement accuracy improves; not a revenue-size claim

risk.note: Setting toggle.

prerequisites: Email platform settings for automatic UTM parameters
steps: Turn on automatically add UTM parameters to links at the account level.
Confirm each flow and campaign template inherits it.
Send a test email and confirm UTM parameters appear in the link.
Confirm the profile shows the open and click with the UTM attached.

test.method: Not a split test; a tracking accuracy check.
test.measure: Share of flow and campaign emails with UTM tracking confirmed on
test.read_point: During account setup and after any template change

title: Set flow first-delays to match the stage, not the platform default
hypothesis: If site abandonment fires in 1 to 4 hours, browse in 30 minutes to 2 hours, and cart or checkout in 15 minutes to 2 hours, then recovery revenue rises because the platform's slower defaults, such as a 4-hour cart delay, let intent cool off first.

signal.check: Any recovery flow still uses the platform default delay, such as a 4-hour cart delay or a 3-day welcome delay.

risk.note: Delay setting change only.

prerequisites: List of current first-delay settings per flow
steps: List the first delay for every recovery flow.
Set site abandonment to 1 to 4 hours.
Set browse abandonment to 30 minutes to 2 hours.
Set cart and checkout to 15 minutes to 2 hours.
Test tighter delays against the new baseline in the flow A/B test process.

test.method: Manual 50/50 split test of 2 delay options per flow, judged on placed order rate and revenue.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, about 2 weeks

title: Hold discounts back to later flow emails, lead with reminder and proof first
hypothesis: If a flow's first emails carry a reminder, founder check-in, social proof and objection handling, and the discount only appears in email 4 or 5 with a real deadline, then margin is protected because the flow does not give away a discount to people who would have bought anyway.
does_not_apply_when: The welcome code, already promised by the popup, which every welcome email should remind

signal.check: A recovery flow offers a discount in email 1 or 2, or offers it to a past buyer with no deadline.

risk.note: Content reorder within existing flows.

prerequisites: Brand discount policy and margin room
steps: Review each recovery flow's discount position.
Move any early discount to email 4 or 5.
Add a reminder, founder check-in and objection-handling email before it.
Route past buyers to a founder support email instead of a fresh discount, or a smaller one if margins allow.

test.method: Compare margin per recovered order before and after the reorder.
test.read_point: After 30 days of the reordered flow

title: Use only real, provable urgency in every discount and deadline
hypothesis: If every deadline uses a unique code or a code that truly expires, then customer trust holds because a fake deadline like a static code that never expires eventually gets noticed and damages future urgency claims.

signal.check: A flow or campaign email uses a static code with a stated expiry, or repeats a resetting countdown timer.

risk.note: Copy and code-generation fix only.

prerequisites: Platform support for unique, expiring discount codes
steps: Find every email using a stated deadline.
Confirm the code referenced actually expires at that time, or switch to a unique per-recipient code.
Remove any resetting countdown timer that does not match a real deadline.
Apply the same check to any future urgency copy.

test.method: Not a split test; a content and platform audit.
test.measure: Share of urgency claims backed by a real, checkable deadline
test.read_point: Before sending any new discount deadline

title: Close key flow sequences with a plain-text founder email
hypothesis: If welcome, cart, post-purchase and win-back sequences end with a plain-text email from a real founder with a reply promise the brand can keep, then response and conversion rise because a plain-text personal email reads as different from the rest of the sequence.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has no founder name, photo or willing signer, or no support capacity to keep a reply promise

signal.check: The end of the welcome, cart, post-purchase or win-back sequence is a designed promotional email instead of a plain-text founder note.

risk.note: Copy change; requires a real reply capacity commitment.

prerequisites: Founder name and willingness to sign
Support reply capacity and hours
steps: Confirm the founder's name and a reply inbox with realistic reply-time capacity.
Write a short plain-text closer for the welcome, cart, post-purchase and win-back sequences.
State a reply promise the brand can actually keep, such as within 24 hours.
Send from the founder's identity, not the brand's promotional sender.

test.method: Compare click and reply rate of the founder closer against the previous last email.

title: Use platform flow templates only for triggers and filters, never their default copy
hypothesis: If templates are used only to inherit triggers, filters and dynamic product tables, and every email's copy is rewritten, then emails feel current and on-brand because template content left as-is tends to look generic and go stale.

signal.check: Any live flow still uses the platform's default template copy, unedited since it was first built.

risk.note: Content rewrite within existing flow structure.

prerequisites: Flow audit identifying template-default copy
steps: Audit every live flow for unedited template copy.
Keep the template's trigger, filters and dynamic product table.
Rewrite every email's subject, body and CTA copy to match the brand.
Recheck flow copy at least once a year as part of the monthly review cadence.

test.method: Not a split test; a content freshness audit.
test.measure: Share of flow emails still on default template copy

title: Test flow email 1's delay before touching its content, on the highest-volume flow first
hypothesis: If we test the delay on email 1 of the highest-volume flow before testing its content, then test effort pays off faster because a small content lift on a low-volume flow's email 6 barely moves total revenue.

signal.check: Recent flow tests changed content or subject lines on a low-volume flow or a late email, with no delay test run on the busiest flow's first email.

risk.note: Test process choice, not a live content change by itself.

prerequisites: Flow entrant volume by flow
steps: Rank flows by monthly entrant volume.
Pick the highest-volume flow.
Test its email 1 delay before testing content.
Only move to content tests once delay is settled.

test.method: Manual 50/50 delay split test, duplicating every downstream email onto both branches.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, about 2 weeks

title: Point the welcome flow trigger at the exact list the popup writes to
hypothesis: If the welcome flow trigger is set to added to the same list the popup writes to, and re-checked whenever a form changes, then new subscribers actually receive the welcome flow, because a mismatched list means the flow never fires for them.

signal.check: A recent form or list change has not been checked against the welcome flow trigger, or a test signup never entered the welcome flow.

risk.note: Trigger verification only.

prerequisites: Access to the popup's list settings and the welcome flow trigger
steps: Open the welcome flow trigger and note the exact list it fires on.
Open the popup form and note the exact list it writes to.
Confirm they match.
Sign up with a test email and confirm entry into the welcome flow.
Re-check this every time a form or list is added or changed.

test.method: Not a split test; a functional check with a test signup.
test.measure: Whether a test signup enters the welcome flow
test.read_point: After any form or list change

title: Filter the welcome flow to first-time subscribers who have never ordered
hypothesis: If the welcome flow filters entrants to placed order 0 times over all time, then margin is protected because past buyers who re-subscribe do not receive the acquisition discount meant for new customers.
does_not_apply_when: The brand sells high-frequency consumables where an all-time exclusion may wrongly block a legitimate repeat subscriber

signal.check: The welcome flow has no placed order filter, so past buyers who re-subscribe receive the first-order discount again.

risk.note: Filter addition only.

prerequisites: Order history data available in the platform
steps: Open the welcome flow's profile filters.
Add placed order equals 0 over all time.
For high-frequency consumables, consider since starting this flow instead of all-time.
Test with a past-buyer profile and confirm they do not enter.

test.method: Not a split test; a filter accuracy check.
test.measure: Share of welcome flow entrants who are true first-time subscribers

title: Front-load the welcome flow into the first 72 hours
hypothesis: If the welcome flow sends most of its emails within the first 72 hours, starting at 0 hours instead of the platform's 3-day default, then welcome conversion rises because day 0 is the highest-converting day and interest fades fast after day 3.

signal.check: Welcome email 1 sends 3 days after signup, or the flow spaces emails 2 or more days apart in the first week.

risk.note: Timing change within an existing flow.

prerequisites: Welcome flow built
steps: Set welcome email 1 to send at 0 hours.
Set email 1B or 2 within the first 24 hours.
Space the remaining emails about 1 day apart through day 3.
Move to 2-day gaps only later in the flow, and only for high AOV products.

test.method: Compare welcome flow placed order rate before and after front-loading.

title: Build a 6 to 8 email welcome sequence with a defined angle per email
hypothesis: If the welcome flow runs 6 to 8 emails, each with 1 clear angle from code delivery through brand story, bestsellers, objections, proof and last chance, then welcome conversion rises because a 1 or 2 email welcome leaves most of the persuasion work undone.

signal.check: The welcome flow has fewer than 6 emails, or several emails cover the same angle.

risk.note: Content build within an existing or new flow.

prerequisites: Bestsellers by first-order share
Reviews tagged by objection
Founder story content
steps: Email 1: code and CTA above the fold, 1 to 3 bestsellers, trust marks.
Email 1B same day: plain-text founder reminder of the code.
Email 2: brand story with substance, founder, mission, quality, sourcing.
Email 3: bestsellers, max 3 to 5, with 1 reason each.
Email 4: objections and us vs them, code deadline at 48 hours if real.
Email 5: reviews that each name an objection, 24 hours left.
Email 6: last chance.
Email 7: plain-text founder extension of 24 hours, only if the code is truly extended.

test.method: Read revenue by email after 30 days; reposition or cut any email earning nothing.
test.measure: other:welcome_flow_placed_order_rate and revenue by email position

title: Keep welcome emails short and repeat the discount code in every one
lever: welcome email length and code repetition
hypothesis: If every welcome email stays under about 100 words and repeats the code, then welcome conversion rises because a shopper skims in 3 seconds and needs the code visible without hunting for it.

signal.check: Any welcome email exceeds a quick skim length, or does not mention the code.

risk.note: Copy trim only.

prerequisites: Existing welcome flow copy
steps: Read each welcome email aloud and time it.
Cut any email that takes longer than a few seconds to skim.
Add the code, bolded, to any email missing it.
Recheck after any copy rewrite.

test.method: Compare click rate and placed order rate before and after trimming length.

title: Set a 10 to 20 percent welcome flow conversion target
hypothesis: If we track welcome flow placed order rate against a 10 percent floor and 20 percent as very good, then underperforming welcome flows get flagged and rebuilt instead of being assumed fine.

signal.check: Welcome flow placed order rate is unknown, or below 10 percent of entrants.

risk.note: Measurement and benchmark, not a change by itself.

prerequisites: Welcome flow entrant and placed order data
steps: Pull welcome flow entrants and placed orders for the last 90 days.
Compute placed order rate.
Compare against the 10 percent floor and 20 percent target.
If below 10 percent, prioritise the welcome flow rebuild ideas above.

test.method: Re-measure monthly after any welcome flow change.

title: Use welcome flow reviews that each name a specific objection
hypothesis: If the welcome flow's review email uses reviews that each name a specific objection instead of generic praise, then conversion rises because 1 review that answers a real doubt outperforms 3 reviews that only say great product.

signal.check: The welcome flow's review-based email uses generic 5-star praise with no named objection or pain point.

risk.note: Content swap within an existing email.

prerequisites: Reviews and testimonials tagged by objection
steps: Pull reviews tagged by the objection they answer.
Pick 1 review per major objection for the welcome flow's proof email.
Replace generic praise-only reviews.
Repeat this check whenever reviews are refreshed.

test.method: Compare click and placed order rate on the proof email before and after the swap.

title: Build a site abandonment flow with a shop-assistant style nudge
hypothesis: If we build a site abandonment flow triggered on active-on-site activity with exit filters for any product view, cart add, checkout or order, then a small extra slice of revenue is recovered from visitors who leave before viewing any specific product.

signal.check: No flow exists for visitors who were active on the site but never viewed a product, added to cart, or checked out.

risk.note: New flow build; no existing flow disrupted.

prerequisites: Active on Site metric or equivalent available in the platform
steps: Create a flow triggered on Active on Site.
Add exit filters: viewed product 0, added to cart 0, checkout started 0, placed order 0, all since starting this flow.
Set re-entry to not in this flow in the last 30 days.
Build 1 email: a shop-assistant nudge such as lost in choices, plus bestsellers or collections and light social proof.

test.method: Compare revenue per recipient of this flow against the site's typical email revenue baseline.

title: Set the site abandonment email to send 1 to 4 hours after activity
hypothesis: If the site abandonment email sends 1 to 4 hours after the visit, and the goal is measured as a product view rather than a purchase, then the flow does its actual job of pushing a browser one step deeper into the funnel.

signal.check: The site abandonment flow, if it exists, has a delay outside 1 to 4 hours or has never been timing-tested.

risk.note: Timing setting change only.

prerequisites: Site abandonment flow built
steps: Set the first and only delay to 2 to 4 hours.
Test 4 hours against 30 minutes if volume allows.
Measure the goal as a product view following the email, not just a purchase.
Adjust based on the test result.

test.method: Manual 50/50 delay split test.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, about 2 weeks

title: Keep the site abandonment flow live during deliverability repair
hypothesis: If the site abandonment flow stays on during a deliverability repair period while other lower-intent sends pause, then a small amount of high-intent revenue is preserved because the flow is small and targets people who were just active on the site.

signal.check: A deliverability repair is underway and every flow, including site abandonment, has been paused.

risk.note: Flow status toggle only.

prerequisites: Deliverability repair ladder underway
steps: During repair, keep welcome, browse, cart, checkout, post-purchase and site abandonment flows live.
Pause all other flows and campaigns per the repair ladder.
Recheck site abandonment volume is small enough not to slow the repair.

test.method: Not a split test; a repair-ladder configuration choice.
test.measure: Deliverability tab open rate trend during repair

title: Build the browse abandonment flow with the added-to-cart filter added by hand
hypothesis: If the browse abandonment flow triggers on Viewed Product and adds the added-to-cart filter the default template is missing, then people who already added an item to their cart stop getting a redundant browse email meant for people who did not.

signal.check: The browse abandonment flow's template is missing an added-to-cart exit filter, or uses the platform's generic add-to-cart API metric instead of the storefront-native one.

risk.note: Filter addition to an existing or new flow.

prerequisites: Viewed Product metric confirmed live
steps: Create the flow on the Viewed Product trigger.
Add added to cart 0, checkout started 0, placed order 0, all since starting this flow.
Use the storefront-native added-to-cart metric, not the generic API one.
Set re-entry to not in this flow in the last 30 days.

test.method: Preview with 2 profiles, 1 that added to cart and 1 that did not, and confirm only the second enters.
test.measure: Whether cart-adding profiles are correctly excluded

title: Set browse abandonment's first delay to 30 minutes to 2 hours
hypothesis: If the browse abandonment flow's first delay is 30 minutes to 2 hours instead of the platform's slower default, then more browsers return while the product is still fresh in mind.

signal.check: The browse abandonment flow uses the platform's default delay, or has never been timing-tested.

risk.note: Timing setting change only.

prerequisites: Browse abandonment flow built
steps: Set the first delay to 45 minutes to 1 hour to start.
Test 45 minutes vs 2 hours if volume allows.
Space the following emails about 1 day apart.

test.method: Manual 50/50 delay split test.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, about 2 weeks

title: Build a 4 to 6 email browse sequence that links to the product, not the homepage
hypothesis: If the browse sequence runs light reminder, risk reversal, product reviews, then a small discount or subscribe-and-save, then a plain-text closer, all linking to the specific product, then browse-to-cart conversion rises because it treats browsing as mid-funnel persuasion, not lost-sale recovery.

signal.check: The browse flow has fewer than 4 emails, opens with a discount instead of trust content, or links to the homepage instead of the viewed product.

risk.note: Content build within existing flow structure.

prerequisites: Reviews tagged by objection
Subscribe-and-save option if applicable
steps: Email 1: light reminder with the viewed item and 4 related products.
Email 2: risk reversal and objections.
Email 3: product-specific reviews.
Email 4: small discount with a 48-hour deadline, or subscribe-and-save for replenishables.
Optional email 5: plain-text 24-hour closer.
Link every image and button to the product URL, never the homepage.

test.method: Compare click-through and cart-add rate before and after the sequence rebuild.

title: Skip the new vs returning split in browse abandonment by default
hypothesis: If browse abandonment sends the same ladder to everyone regardless of buyer status, then build and maintenance time drops because browsers are low intent even if they bought before, and splitting adds complexity for little gain.
does_not_apply_when: Margins cannot support any discount to past buyers; split by buyer status on the discount email only

signal.check: The browse flow already branches by new vs returning with no clear margin reason for the split.

risk.note: Simplifies an existing flow; can be re-split later if margin requires it.

prerequisites: Current browse flow structure
steps: Review whether the browse flow splits by buyer status.
If margin allows any discount to past buyers, merge the branches into 1 ladder.
If margin cannot support that, keep the split only on the discount email.

test.method: Not a split test; a flow simplification decision checked against margin.
test.measure: gross_margin impact of the discount email

title: Build 2 separate flows: Added to Cart and Checkout Started
hypothesis: If we build a real Added to Cart flow alongside a separate Checkout Started flow, then abandoned-cart revenue rises because most accounts only have a checkout flow mislabeled as a cart flow, leaving cart-only abandoners with nothing.

signal.check: The account has only 1 flow named abandoned cart, and its trigger reads Checkout Started rather than Added to Cart.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source notes about 90 percent of audited accounts lack a real cart flow

risk.note: New flow build alongside the existing checkout flow.

prerequisites: Added to Cart metric confirmed live (see the ATC metric idea)
steps: Open every flow named abandoned cart and read its actual trigger.
If the trigger is Checkout Started, rename that flow Abandoned checkout.
Build a new flow triggered on Added to Cart, with a checkout-started exit filter.
Confirm both flows exist and cover the 2 distinct drop-off points.

test.method: Compare recovered revenue before and after adding the missing cart flow.

title: Confirm the Added to Cart metric actually fires before building on it
hypothesis: If we confirm the Added to Cart metric is firing with recent events before building the cart flow on it, then the flow works from day 1 instead of silently never triggering because the integration was API-only or the snippet was never installed.

signal.check: No Added to Cart metric with recent events appears in the platform's metrics list.

risk.note: Verification and, if needed, a snippet install.

prerequisites: Access to the platform's metrics dashboard and theme code
steps: Check the metrics tab for a storefront-native Added to Cart metric with recent events.
If absent, install the platform's onsite snippet in the theme.
Add to cart with a test profile carrying a tracking parameter.
Confirm the Added to Cart event appears on that test profile.

test.method: Not a split test; a functional verification step.
test.measure: Whether a test add-to-cart produces the event

title: Set cart and checkout re-entry windows from the product's repurchase interval
hypothesis: If the cart flow's re-entry window is set from the brand's own repurchase interval, 7 days or less for weekly consumables and 14 to 30 days otherwise, then repeat abandoners get a fresh nudge at the right pace instead of being locked out too long or hit too often.

signal.check: Cart and checkout flow re-entry windows use a flat default, such as 30 days, regardless of the product's actual repurchase cycle.

risk.note: Setting change only.

prerequisites: Repurchase interval for the product or category
steps: Pull the typical repurchase interval for the product.
For weekly consumables, set re-entry to 7 days or less.
For everything else, set re-entry to 14 to 30 days.
Set the checkout flow's re-entry a little tighter than the cart flow's.

test.method: Not a split test; a settings check against known repurchase data.

title: Set cart and checkout first delay to 15 minutes to 1 hour
hypothesis: If cart and checkout flows send their first email 15 minutes to 1 hour after abandonment instead of the platform's 4-hour default, then recovered revenue rises because the platform default is described as way too long.

signal.check: The cart or checkout flow's first delay is at or near the platform's 4-hour default.

risk.note: Timing setting change only.

prerequisites: Cart and checkout flows built
steps: Set the first delay to 30 to 45 minutes to start.
Test 15 minutes vs 1 hour, then later 2 vs 4 hours if useful.
Apply the winning delay to both cart and checkout flows separately.

test.method: Manual 50/50 delay split test on 1 flow at a time.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, about 2 weeks

title: Build cart and checkout at 6 to 8 emails over about 10 days
hypothesis: If cart and checkout flows run 6 to 8 emails over about 10 days instead of 1 or 2 short sends, then recovered revenue rises because too few emails let buyers off the hook before their decision cycle ends, while 14 to 20 emails draws complaints.

signal.check: The cart or checkout flow has 1 or 2 emails, or has grown past 12 to 14 emails.

risk.note: Adding emails raises send pressure; watch unsubscribes.

prerequisites: Existing cart and checkout flow content
steps: Count the current number of emails in the cart and checkout flows.
If under 3, add emails to reach 6 to 8 spread over about 10 days.
If over about 12 to 14, cut to the strongest 6 to 8.
Watch unsubscribe rate by email position after the change.

test.method: Compare recovered revenue and unsubscribe rate before and after resizing the sequence.

title: Sequence cart and checkout content: reminder, founder check-in, objections, proof, then a buyer-status split
hypothesis: If the cart and checkout flows follow reminder, founder check-in, objections, product-specific proof, then last chance with a buyer-status discount split, then recovered revenue rises because each email answers the specific reason a real shopper stalls at that step.

signal.check: Cart or checkout emails jump straight to a discount or repeat the same generic reminder instead of building through objections and proof.

risk.note: Content rebuild within existing flow structure.

prerequisites: Objection list with brand proof for each
steps: Email 1 at first delay: you left this behind, dynamic item, risk reversal, no discount.
Email 2 next day: plain-text founder check-in, did you run into any issues, with 1 differentiator.
Email 3 next day: objections answered with USPs, price, shipping, fit, quality.
Email 4: product-specific testimonials.
Email 5 around day 5: last chance with alternative products.
Split by placed order at least once: buyers get a founder support email, non-buyers get a discount with 48 hours then a 24-hour plain-text closer.

test.method: Compare recovered revenue before and after the content rebuild.

title: Restrict cart and checkout discounts to never-bought or 60 to 90 day lapsed customers
hypothesis: If cart and checkout discounts only go to people who never bought or have not bought in 60 to 90 days, then margin holds because a discount to a recent buyer generates revenue while quietly destroying margin on an order that would have happened anyway.

signal.check: Cart or checkout discount emails go to everyone regardless of purchase history, including recent buyers.

risk.note: Filter addition on the discount branch.

prerequisites: Order history and discount policy
steps: Add a filter on the discount branch: placed order 0 over all time, or last order 60 to 90 days ago or more.
Route everyone else to the no-discount founder support branch.
Confirm the split works with a test profile that ordered recently.

test.method: Compare margin per recovered order before and after the eligibility restriction.

title: Build separate, correctly linked dynamic item blocks for cart and checkout
hypothesis: If the cart flow's dynamic item block links to the cart page and the checkout flow's links to the actual checkout URL, built and tested separately, then click-through rises because a copied block that links to the wrong page sends people back to an empty cart instead of finishing their order.

signal.check: The checkout flow's dynamic item block was copied from the cart flow, or its links do not point to the live checkout URL.

risk.note: Block rebuild within existing flows.

prerequisites: Access to each flow's dynamic block editor
steps: Rebuild the checkout flow's dynamic block using the checkout event's own variables.
Link every image and button in the checkout block to the checkout URL variable.
Keep the cart block linking to the cart page or specific item.
Preview each block with several real profiles to confirm images, names, prices and links load correctly.

test.method: Not a split test; a functional accuracy check with multiple test profiles.
test.measure: Whether dynamic blocks show correct items and links
test.read_point: Before publishing and during the flow audit checklist

title: Answer checkout-specific objections, offer free shipping where shipping cost is the blocker
hypothesis: If the checkout flow answers the actual checkout objection, offering free shipping instead of a percent discount when a shipping fee was the blocker, then checkout completion rises because the fix matches the real reason the shopper stopped.

signal.check: The checkout flow uses the same generic percent-off offer as the cart flow, with no shipping-specific alternative.

risk.note: Offer swap within an existing flow.

prerequisites: Shipping cost and AOV to judge whether free shipping is affordable
steps: Identify the shipping fee shown at checkout.
Where AOV and margin allow it, offer free shipping instead of a percent discount in the checkout flow.
Rewrite checkout copy to name the objection directly, price, payment, delivery time or fit.
Keep the cart flow's offer separate from the checkout flow's.

test.method: A/B test free shipping vs percent discount on the checkout flow.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, about 2 weeks

title: Split cart and checkout emails 3 and 4 by product collection
hypothesis: If cart and checkout objection and proof emails split by the item's main collection, showing collection-specific reviews and objections, then relevance and conversion rise because generic proof reads weaker than proof tied to what the shopper was actually looking at.
does_not_apply_when: The catalogue has too many collections to split cleanly; keep to a few main collections

signal.check: Emails 3 and 4 of the cart or checkout flow show the same generic proof regardless of which collection the abandoned item belongs to.

risk.note: Adds trigger-based splits to existing emails.

prerequisites: A short list of the brand's main collections
steps: Identify the brand's few main product collections.
Build a split in emails 3 and 4 by collection, not by individual product.
Write collection-specific proof and objection content for each branch.
Avoid building more than a handful of splits.

test.method: Compare click and conversion rate on the split version against the generic version.

title: Build post-purchase with cancelled-order exit and subscription routing
hypothesis: If the post-purchase flow filters out cancelled orders and routes subscription or B2B customers to their own flow, then post-purchase content stays relevant because a cancelled buyer or a subscriber does not get the standard first-order cross-sell track.

signal.check: The post-purchase flow has no cancelled-order exit filter, or subscription and B2B customers receive the same content as one-off retail buyers.

risk.note: Filter and routing addition to an existing flow.

prerequisites: Subscription and B2B customer tags
steps: Add cancelled order 0 since starting this flow as an exit filter.
Add a filter or split routing subscription and B2B customers to their own track.
Test with a cancelled-order profile and confirm they exit.
Test with a subscription profile and confirm they route separately.

test.method: Not a split test; a functional filter check.
test.measure: Whether cancelled and subscription profiles are correctly routed

title: Send the first post-purchase email 10 to 30 minutes after order, plain text from the founder
hypothesis: If the first post-purchase email sends 10 to 30 minutes after the order as a plain-text founder note, then buyer confidence rises right after purchase because it lands after the order confirmation rather than at 0 minutes or a full day later.

signal.check: The post-purchase flow's first email sends at 0 minutes, before the order confirmation, or waits a full day with no fixed reasoning.

risk.note: Timing setting change only.

prerequisites: Founder name and reply capacity
steps: Set the post-purchase flow's first delay to 10 to 30 minutes after the order event.
Write it as a plain-text thank-you from the founder.
Confirm the order confirmation email fires first, not after.

test.method: Compare open and click rate at 30 minutes vs 4 hours as a delay test.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, about 2 weeks

title: Split post-purchase content between first-time and returning buyers
hypothesis: If first-time buyers get a reassurance and soft cross-sell track while returning buyers get a loyalty track with no acquisition offer, then repeat purchase rate rises because each group gets the message that actually fits their relationship with the brand.

signal.check: The post-purchase flow sends the same content to first-time and returning buyers, including sending a first-order discount to a repeat customer.

risk.note: Adds a conditional split to an existing flow.

prerequisites: Order count data per customer
steps: Add a conditional split: placed order equals 1 over all time.
First-time track: thanks for trusting us, reassurance, what happens next, soft cross-sell.
Returning track: thanks for loyalty, no acquisition offer, subscribe-and-save or loyalty push, cross-sell.
Confirm with a 1st-order and a repeat-order test profile.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase rate before and after the split.

title: Build the 6 to 8 step first-time post-purchase content sequence
hypothesis: If the first-time post-purchase track runs founder thank-you, shipping update with add-ons, how-to content, social follow, loyalty benefit, review request, and a founder check-in, then repeat purchase rate rises because each stage reduces remorse or return risk and builds toward the next order.

signal.check: The first-time post-purchase track has fewer than 5 emails or skips how-to content, loyalty introduction, or a founder check-in.

risk.note: Content build within an existing or new flow.

prerequisites: Delivery times per region
How-to content by product or category
Loyalty program details if any
steps: Email 1 at 10 to 30 minutes: founder thank-you.
Email 2 at 1 to 2 days: order on its way, add-ons, reduce remorse.
Email 3 after delivery: how to get the most from the product, split by product or category.
Email 4 about day 7: follow 1 social channel.
Email 5 after delivery: loyalty program with the benefit stated at once.
Email 6 about 3 days later: review request, optional thank-you code.
Email 7 at 1 to 2 weeks after delivery: founder check-in, how did everything go.
Optional email 8: cross-sell with a 48-hour code then a 24-hour plain-text closer.

test.method: Read revenue and repeat rate by email after 60 days; reposition or cut weak emails.

title: Focus post-purchase effort on the 30-day window after order 1
hypothesis: If we concentrate post-purchase content and offers inside the first 30 days after order 1, then the first-to-second purchase rate rises because most repeat purchases happen in that window, and it is the hardest step to get right.

signal.check: Post-purchase content is spread evenly over 60 or more days with no extra weight on the first 30.

risk.note: Reweighting of existing content timing.

prerequisites: Days-between-order-1-and-order-2 data
steps: Pull days between order 1 and order 2 for recent customers.
Confirm most repeats happen within 30 days.
Concentrate the strongest post-purchase content and any first cross-sell push inside that window.
Move lower-priority content later.

test.method: Compare first-to-second purchase rate before and after reweighting content timing.

title: Match post-purchase how-to content to what the customer actually bought
hypothesis: If the how-to email in post-purchase is split by product or category, giving care instructions for apparel and setup guides for technical products, then returns drop because customers understand how to use what they bought instead of guessing.

signal.check: The post-purchase how-to email is generic across all products, with no split for apparel, technical products or other categories.

risk.note: Content split within an existing email.

prerequisites: How-to content by product or category
steps: List the brand's main product categories.
Write how-to content matched to each: care instructions, setup guides, sizing tips, as needed.
Split the post-purchase how-to email by the category of the item bought.
Track return rate by category before and after.

test.method: Compare return rate by category before and after the split.

title: Hand review-request timing to the connected reviews app once it has one
hypothesis: If the review request runs on the connected reviews app's own trigger once one exists, and stops asking once a review event fires, then customers stop getting duplicate or mistimed review requests from 2 different systems.
does_not_apply_when: No reviews app is connected

signal.check: Both the email platform and a separate reviews app send review requests to the same customer with no coordination.

risk.note: Coordination change; removes a duplicate send.

prerequisites: A connected reviews app with its own trigger
steps: Confirm the reviews app can send its own request on its own trigger.
Turn off or shorten the email platform's separate review-request email.
Add a filter so the post-purchase flow stops asking once a review event exists.
Confirm non-reviewers can still receive any thank-you code tied to that step.

test.method: Not a split test; a coordination check to remove duplicate asks.

title: Build a refunds segment with a short, low-pressure post-refund check-in
hypothesis: If refunded customers exit cross-sell and review-request messaging and instead get a brief, no-pressure check-in, then trust holds because a refunded buyer does not get asked to buy more or rate a product they just returned.

signal.check: Refunded customers still receive cross-sell or review-request emails from the standard post-purchase track.

risk.note: New segment and short flow; verify against brand data before use.

prerequisites: A refunds segment or metric in the platform
steps: Build a refunds segment using the platform's refund event or metric.
Exclude refunded customers from cross-sell and review-request sends.
Send a short, no-pressure check-in instead, asking if anything else is needed.
Route any reply to support, not marketing.

test.method: Not a split test; verify against brand data and support feedback before wider use.
