test.read_point: After the first 20 to 30 refunds under the new flow

title: Build dedicated subscription lifecycle emails: charge reminder, pause-or-skip, failed payment
hypothesis: If subscription customers get their own charge-reminder, pause-or-skip save flow, and failed-payment recovery emails, then subscription churn drops because subscribers get built-for-them messaging instead of being merely excluded from acquisition flows with nothing to replace it.

signal.check: Subscription customers are excluded from acquisition flows but have no dedicated charge-reminder, pause-or-skip, or failed-payment email.

risk.note: New flows; verify against the subscription platform's billing cadence and dunning settings.

prerequisites: Subscription platform, billing cadence, and dunning settings
steps: Build a charge-reminder email a few days before each renewal charge.
Build a pause-or-skip save flow triggered before a likely cancellation point.
Build a failed-payment recovery flow triggered on a declined charge.
Confirm timing against the subscription platform's own dunning settings to avoid duplicate messages.

test.method: Track subscription churn and save-flow conversion before and after launch.

title: Split gift purchases into a buyer thread and a recipient thread
hypothesis: If gift orders trigger a buyer thread covering delivery and a thank-you note option, plus a separate recipient thread covering product care and the account once the recipient is known, then both people get relevant content instead of the buyer receiving messaging meant for the person who will actually use the product.
does_not_apply_when: The platform cannot identify gift orders or capture recipient details separately

signal.check: Gift orders trigger the same post-purchase track as a normal order, with no separate recipient messaging.

risk.note: New flow; verify recipient data capture is possible before building.

prerequisites: A way to flag gift orders and capture recipient contact details
steps: Flag gift orders at checkout or in the order data.
Build a buyer thread: delivery update, gifting confirmation, an optional thank-you note.
Build a recipient thread once the recipient is known: product care, how-to, account and return path.
Exclude the buyer from the recipient's cross-sell and review-request messaging.

test.method: Not a split test; a new flow checked against gift order volume and complaint rate.
test.measure: csat and return rate on gift orders
test.read_point: After the first holiday or gifting season with the flow live

title: Add a fit-check email before the review request for size-dependent products
hypothesis: If a fit-check email asks did it fit before the review request, then returns drop because a bad fit reaches support first instead of turning straight into a return or a bad review.
does_not_apply_when: The product category has no size or fit variation

signal.check: The brand sells size- or fit-dependent products and the post-purchase track goes straight from delivery to a review request with no fit check.

risk.note: Single email insertion into an existing flow; verify against brand data before use.

prerequisites: Support capacity to handle fit-check replies
steps: Insert a short email after delivery asking did it fit, with a 1-click yes or no.
Route a no answer to support with sizing help before a return label is offered.
Route a yes answer into the normal review-request email.
Track how many fit-check replies turn into an exchange instead of a return.

test.method: Compare return rate for size-dependent products before and after the fit-check email.

title: Add a shipping-delay update email for international orders
hypothesis: If international orders get a longer, honest delivery-expectation email plus a customs or delay notice where relevant, then support tickets drop because international customers are told the real timeline instead of receiving the same domestic delivery message.
does_not_apply_when: The brand ships only domestically

signal.check: International orders receive the same post-purchase shipping timing and copy as domestic orders, with no country-specific delivery expectation.

risk.note: New email branch; verify shipping times and carriers by country before writing copy.

prerequisites: Shipping times and carriers by country
steps: Pull shipping times by country from the fulfilment or carrier data.
Write a delivery-expectation email that states the real, longer timeline for international orders.
Add a customs or delay notice where the brand ships across borders that commonly hold packages.
Route international orders to this branch instead of the domestic timing.

test.method: Compare shipping-related support tickets before and after the change, for international orders.

title: Time replenishment reminders to days of supply plus delivery time
hypothesis: If the replenishment reminder fires a few days before the product is expected to run out, based on days of supply plus delivery time, then reorder rate rises because the reminder lands while the customer can still act before running out.
does_not_apply_when: The product is a 1-time purchase with no replenishment cycle

signal.check: No replenishment reminder exists for a consumable or replenishable product, or it fires on a flat schedule unrelated to the product's days of supply.

risk.note: New flow using existing order data.

prerequisites: Days of supply per product
Typical delivery time
steps: Compute days of supply for each replenishable product.
Add delivery time and subtract a few days as a buffer.
Trigger the reminder that many days after the order, with no offer at first.
Write the email as are you running low, reorder here.

test.method: Compare reorder rate for customers who received the reminder against those who did not, or before and after launch.

title: Use the platform's predictive next-order date as the replenishment trigger
hypothesis: If the replenishment flow triggers on the platform's own predicted next-order date once enough order history exists, then timing accuracy improves because the trigger adapts per customer instead of using 1 fixed day-count for everyone.
does_not_apply_when: The brand does not yet have enough order history for predictions to populate

signal.check: Replenishment timing uses a single fixed day count for all customers, and the platform offers a predictive next-order date property that is unused.

risk.note: Trigger swap on an existing or new flow.

prerequisites: Enough order history for the platform's prediction to populate
steps: Confirm the platform's predicted next-order date property is populating for customers.
Build a flow triggered on that date property, starting at midday recipient local time, never repeating.
Add placed order 0 since starting this flow as a filter.
Add a short delay after the trigger date before the first email.

test.method: Compare reorder rate on the predictive trigger against the fixed-day trigger.

title: Set the win-back wait time from the brand's own median and mean days between orders
hypothesis: If the win-back flow's wait time is set from the brand's own median and mean days between orders, or twice the average interval, instead of the platform's default, then win-back timing matches real customer behaviour instead of an arbitrary default that may fire too early or too late.

signal.check: The win-back flow uses the platform's default wait time, such as 75 or 90 days, with no check against the brand's own order data.

risk.note: Timing setting change using existing order data.

prerequisites: Median and mean days between orders
steps: Pull days between order 1 and order 2, and later orders, for recent customers.
Compute the median and mean.
Set the win-back wait time to a point between them, or twice the average interval.
Sanity check the number against days of supply plus shipping time for consumables.

test.method: Compare win-back conversion rate at the new wait time against the platform default.

title: Space win-back emails 3 to 7 days apart, never daily
hypothesis: If win-back emails are spaced 3 to 7 days apart instead of daily, then complaint and unsubscribe rate stay lower because lapsed buyers are quicker to complain about frequent email than an engaged customer would be.

signal.check: Win-back flow emails send with 1-day gaps or less.

risk.note: Timing setting change only.

prerequisites: Win-back flow built
steps: Review the current gap between win-back emails.
Set gaps to 3 to 7 days.
Watch unsubscribe rate on the win-back flow specifically after the change.

test.method: Compare unsubscribe rate before and after widening the gaps.

title: Build the win-back sequence: no-discount nudge, reminder, coded offer, closer
hypothesis: If win-back opens with a no-discount it's been a while email, then a reminder, then a unique coded offer with a 48-hour deadline, then a plain-text closer, then win-back conversion rises because the sequence earns attention before asking for the sale.

signal.check: The win-back flow opens with a discount in email 1, or has only 1 or 2 emails.

risk.note: Content build within existing or new flow.

prerequisites: Win-back wait time set from the brand's own data
steps: Email 1: it's been a while, no discount, new arrivals.
Email 2, 3 to 7 days later: reminder.
Email 3: unique dynamic code with a 48-hour deadline.
Email 4: 24-hour plain-text closer.
Optional email 5, about 2 weeks later: bigger second offer.

test.method: Compare win-back conversion rate before and after the sequence rebuild.

title: Add past lapsed profiles into a new win-back flow with a static code
hypothesis: If a newly built win-back flow adds past lapsed profiles immediately using a static code, then those customers start receiving win-back messages right away instead of waiting the full trigger delay to enter naturally.

signal.check: A new win-back flow was just built, and past lapsed customers will only enter it after they cross the wait threshold again in the future.

risk.note: One-time backfill action.

prerequisites: A static discount code for the backfill, since dynamic per-recipient codes may not apply to a bulk add
steps: Identify the flow's add past profiles or equivalent bulk-entry function.
Create a static code to use for this one-time backfill.
Add existing lapsed profiles into the flow throughout its steps, not just at step 1.
Confirm the code works and expires as intended.

test.method: Track win-back revenue from the backfilled cohort over the following 30 to 60 days.

title: Give high-CLV lapsed customers a stronger win-back offer
hypothesis: If lapsed customers with historic or predicted lifetime value above a set threshold get a stronger, more personal win-back offer, then high-value win-back revenue rises because the standard offer under-invests in the customers worth the most to recover.

signal.check: The win-back flow sends the same offer to every lapsed customer regardless of historic spend or predicted lifetime value.

risk.note: Adds a split to the existing win-back flow.

prerequisites: Historic or predicted lifetime value data per customer
steps: Set a lifetime value threshold that marks a high-value customer for the brand.
Add a split in the win-back flow for customers above that threshold.
Build a stronger, more personal offer for that branch.
Keep the standard sequence for everyone else.

test.method: Compare win-back conversion rate for the high-value branch against the standard branch.

title: Define the sunset trigger as zero engagement across a fixed window with a minimum-sends floor
hypothesis: If the sunset trigger requires zero opens, clicks and site activity across a 120-day window, with at least 6 emails received in that window, then the sunset flow only catches people who had a fair chance and still never engaged, rather than people who simply were not sent enough email.

signal.check: No sunset trigger segment exists, or it uses OR logic, has no minimum-sends floor, or uses a window under 90 days or over 180 days with no stated reason.

risk.note: Segment definition change; feeds into the sunset flow, not a direct suppression.

prerequisites: Purchase cycle data to decide whether past buyers are exempt
steps: Build a segment for 0 opens, 0 clicks, 0 orders, 0 checkouts, 0 carts, 0 views and 0 site visits in the last 120 days.
Add received at least 6 emails in that 120-day window.
Decide whether to exempt past buyers of a slow-cycle product, based on the brand's purchase cycle.
Point this segment at the sunset flow's trigger.

test.method: Not a split test; a segment definition check against list health.
test.measure: Size of the sunset trigger segment as a share of the list
test.read_point: Monthly, as part of the suppression review

title: Use AND, not OR, on the sunset flow's opened and clicked filters
hypothesis: If the sunset flow filter requires opened 0 AND clicked 0 since starting this flow, then people who open but never click stop wrongly re-entering the sunset sequence every cycle, because OR logic would keep catching them.

signal.check: The sunset flow's profile filters use OR logic between opened and clicked, or have not been checked recently.

risk.note: Filter logic fix only.

prerequisites: Access to the sunset flow's filter settings
steps: Open the sunset flow's profile filters.
Confirm opened email 0 times AND clicked email 0 times, both since starting this flow.
Fix the logic if it currently reads as OR.
Test with a profile that opens but does not click and confirm they are not re-sunsetted.

test.method: Not a split test; a logic correctness check.

title: Run a 3-email, 5-day-gap sunset sequence before marking unengaged
hypothesis: If the sunset flow runs 3 plain-text emails with 5-day gaps, aiming for an open or click, before marking the profile unengaged and suppressing it, then a share of the list re-engages instead of being suppressed without one last real attempt.

signal.check: No sunset flow exists, or unengaged profiles are suppressed directly with no final win-back attempt.

risk.note: New flow build using the sunset trigger segment.

prerequisites: Sunset trigger segment defined
steps: Email 1: still interested, if not, unsubscribe here.
Email 2, 5 days later: strongest offer with a unique code.
Email 3, 5 days later: we will remove you unless you click below to keep receiving updates.
After email 3, update the profile property to unengaged true.
Aim the goal at an open or click, not a sale.

test.method: Track the share of the sunset flow's entrants who re-engage before suppression.
test.measure: Share of sunset entrants who open or click
test.read_point: After each monthly sunset cohort completes

title: Suppress spam marks, bounces and the unengaged segment monthly
hypothesis: If spam marks, hard bounces, repeated soft bounces and the unengaged segment are suppressed every month, then deliverability holds because the platform bills and reputation systems both react to a growing pool of dead or angry profiles.

signal.check: No suppression has run in the last 30 days, or spam and bounce segments have grown without being suppressed.

risk.note: Suppression may not be reversible on every platform; check unsuppress rules first.

prerequisites: Spam, bounce and unengaged segments built
Platform's unsuppress rules checked
steps: Build or confirm segments for spam marks, hard bounces, 4 or more soft bounces, and unengaged.
Check the platform's unsuppress rules before running suppression.
Suppress each segment monthly, either through a bulk action or an export and import.
Log the date of the last suppression run.

test.method: Not a split test; track deliverability metrics over successive monthly suppression cycles.

title: Trigger back-in-stock emails only from a real restock event
hypothesis: If back-in-stock emails only fire from the platform's real subscribed-to-back-in-stock metric on genuine new inventory, and campaign-style restock announcements are used only for real restocks, then customer trust holds because no one gets told an item restocked when it did not.

signal.check: A back-in-stock or restock email has been sent for an item that did not actually restock.

risk.note: Process and trigger check.

prerequisites: Real-time inventory data connected to the email platform
steps: Confirm the back-in-stock flow uses the platform's real subscribed-to-back-in-stock metric.
Confirm the trigger only fires when inventory actually increases from zero.
Use the campaign restock announcement type only for genuine new inventory.
Never simulate a sell-out or restock to create urgency.

test.method: Not a split test; an honesty and trigger-accuracy check.
test.measure: Whether every back-in-stock send matches a real inventory event

title: Time the review-request email about 3 days after delivery
hypothesis: If the review-request email sends about 3 days after the loyalty email, and after delivery is confirmed, then review response rate rises because the customer has had enough time to actually use the product before being asked.

signal.check: The review request sends on a fixed day count from order date instead of from delivery, or before the customer would have used the product.

risk.note: Timing setting change only.

prerequisites: Delivery confirmation data or estimate
steps: Confirm the post-purchase flow can trigger relative to delivery, not just order date.
Set the review request to send about 3 days after the loyalty email, which itself follows delivery.
Allow non-reviewers to still receive any thank-you code tied to this step.

test.method: Compare review response rate before and after the timing fix.

title: Build a birthday flow off the loyalty app's birthday event with a live points balance
hypothesis: If the birthday email triggers on the loyalty app's own birthday event and shows the customer's live points balance, then engagement rises because the message feels personal and accurate instead of generic.
does_not_apply_when: No loyalty app is connected and no birthday data is collected

signal.check: No birthday flow exists despite a connected loyalty app with birthday and points data available.

risk.note: New flow build.

prerequisites: Connected loyalty app with birthday and points data
steps: Confirm the loyalty app exposes a birthday event and a points-balance property.
Build a flow triggered on the birthday event.
Personalise the email with the live points balance.
Preview with 2 different profiles to confirm the numbers actually differ.

test.method: Not a split test; track engagement on the new flow after launch.
test.read_point: After the first full birthday cycle, about 12 months, or after 30 days for a large enough list

title: Build a points-earned flow off the loyalty app's points-earned event
hypothesis: If a points-earned email confirms the new balance right when points are earned, then loyalty program engagement rises because customers get a timely, specific update instead of no confirmation at all.
does_not_apply_when: No loyalty app is connected

signal.check: The loyalty app fires a points-earned event with no corresponding email, so customers only see their balance if they log in.

risk.note: New flow build using existing loyalty app data.

prerequisites: Connected loyalty app with a points-earned event
steps: Confirm the loyalty app exposes a points-earned event.
Build a flow triggered on that event.
Confirm the new balance in the email body.
Preview with a real profile to check the balance shown is accurate.

test.method: Not a split test; track click rate and loyalty program activity after launch.

title: Build a tier-up flow off the loyalty app's tier-change event
hypothesis: If a tier-up email states the new tier's benefit right when a customer's loyalty tier changes, then loyalty engagement rises because the customer immediately knows what they earned instead of finding out by accident.
does_not_apply_when: No loyalty app with tiers is connected

signal.check: The loyalty app fires a tier-change event with no corresponding email.

risk.note: New flow build using existing loyalty app data.

prerequisites: Connected loyalty app with a tier-change event
steps: Confirm the loyalty app exposes a tier-change event.
Build a flow triggered on that event.
State the new tier's benefit clearly and immediately in the email.
Preview with a profile that just changed tiers.

test.method: Not a split test; track click rate and tier-benefit redemption after launch.

title: Build a reward-redeemed flow off the loyalty app's redemption event
hypothesis: If a redemption email confirms what was redeemed and how to use it, then redemption follow-through rises because the customer has a clear reference instead of relying on memory or a separate account login.
does_not_apply_when: No loyalty app with redeemable rewards is connected

signal.check: The loyalty app fires a redemption event with no corresponding confirmation email.

risk.note: New flow build using existing loyalty app data.

prerequisites: Connected loyalty app with a redemption event
steps: Confirm the loyalty app exposes a redemption event.
Build a flow triggered on that event.
Confirm what was redeemed and explain how to use it, including any code or link.
Preview with a real redemption profile.

test.method: Not a split test; track redemption follow-through after launch.
test.measure: Share of redemptions actually used within their validity window

title: Keep 1 master email list and 1 SMS list, send to segments, not lists
hypothesis: If the account keeps exactly 1 master email list and 1 SMS list, and every campaign sends to a dynamic segment rather than a static list, then targeting stays flexible because segments update automatically while lists do not.

signal.check: The account has multiple overlapping email lists, or campaigns are sent directly to a list instead of a segment.

expected_effect.size: cleaner targeting, not a list-size claim

risk.note: Consolidating lists needs care to avoid losing consent records.

prerequisites: Audit of every current list and its consent source
steps: List every email and SMS list currently in the account.
Consolidate opt-ins into 1 master email list and 1 master SMS list, preserving consent records.
Rebuild any campaign audience currently pointed at a list to instead use a segment.
Check for the exceptions where a direct list send is genuinely needed.

test.method: Not a split test; a structural audit.
test.measure: Number of active lists vs segments used for sends
test.read_point: During account setup or the next full audit

title: Join every segment's can-receive-email-marketing condition with AND, never OR
hypothesis: If every segment's base condition uses AND on can receive email marketing rather than OR, then sends stop reaching almost the entire list by accident, because OR at the top level pulls in people the segment was never meant to include.

signal.check: Any segment uses OR to join can receive email marketing with its other conditions, or this has never been checked.

expected_effect.size: corrected segment sizes, not a list-size claim

risk.note: Logic fix on existing segments.

prerequisites: Access to every active segment's condition builder
steps: Open every active segment used for sends.
Check whether can receive email marketing is joined with AND to the rest of the conditions.
Fix any segment using OR at that level.
Recheck the preview count after the fix; it should shrink if the bug was present.

test.method: Not a split test; a logic correctness audit.
test.measure: Segment preview count before and after the AND/OR fix

title: Build the core engaged segment from opens, clicks, orders and site activity
hypothesis: If the engaged segment combines opened, clicked, ordered, checkout-started or active-on-site in the window with a bounce and spam exclusion, and a carve-out for subscribers in the last 14 days, then campaigns reach the right audience because new subscribers are not wrongly dropped and dead profiles are not wrongly included.

signal.check: No formal engaged segment exists, or campaigns send to the whole list or to a static list instead.

risk.note: Segment build; used as the audience for future sends.

prerequisites: Apple privacy open and bot click exclusions available in the platform
steps: Build a condition group with OR: opened, clicked (bot click false), placed order, checkout started, or active on site in the window.
AND can receive email marketing.
AND bounced 0 times and marked spam 0 times over all time.
Add subscribed to list in the last 14 days as an OR so new subscribers are not dropped.
Check the preview count makes sense against total list size.

test.method: Not a split test; compare campaign performance before and after switching to this segment.
test.measure: Campaign click rate and placed order rate to the engaged segment
test.read_point: After the first few campaigns using the new segment

title: Set the engaged-segment window by send type and list health
hypothesis: If the engaged-segment window starts at 90 days for evergreen sends, widens as opens stay high, and narrows to 14 or 30 days only during a deliverability repair, then campaigns reach the right size and quality audience for the situation instead of using 1 fixed window for everything.

signal.check: Only 1 engaged-segment window exists, used for every situation regardless of list health or send type.

risk.note: Cloning the engaged segment at different windows.

prerequisites: Engaged segment defined at a base window
steps: Clone the base engaged segment at 14, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 365 days.
Use 90 days as the default for evergreen campaigns.
Use 14 or 30 days only during a deliverability repair.
Use 365 days only for major sale events.
Widen the default window as open rate on engaged sends climbs above 60 to 70 percent.

test.method: Not a split test; monitor open rate as the trigger for widening the window.
test.measure: Open rate, Apple opens excluded, on engaged sends

title: Widen the engaged window to 365 days for major sale events only
hypothesis: If big sale events, such as an annual sale, send to a 365-day engaged window while evergreen content stays at 90 days, then sale revenue rises because once-a-year shoppers who only re-engage on big moments still get reached.

signal.check: A major annual sale is sent only to the standard 90-day engaged segment, missing once-a-year shoppers.

risk.note: Sending wider raises reach to less-engaged profiles; watch complaint and spam rate closely during the sale.

prerequisites: 365-day engaged segment cloned
steps: Confirm the 365-day engaged segment exists.
Use it as the audience for the brand's biggest annual sale sends only.
Keep evergreen content on the 90-day segment.
Watch spam and unsubscribe rate closely during the wider send.

test.method: Compare sale revenue reached through the 365-day segment against the 90-day segment alone.
test.read_point: During and immediately after the sale event

title: Split prospects vs customers to learn from them, but keep sends to both together
hypothesis: If prospects and customers are split only to learn what converts each, while evergreen campaign content still goes to both combined, then reach stays high because splitting a send into small audiences below a certain list size actually lowers total shots on goal.
does_not_apply_when: The store is well above roughly 20 million dollars a year, where micro-splitting barely shrinks reach

signal.check: Evergreen campaigns are split into small prospect and customer sends instead of 1 combined send, on a list under about 20 million dollars a year in revenue.

risk.note: Send consolidation; personalisation moves inside the email instead.

prerequisites: Prospects and customers segments both defined
steps: Keep prospects (placed order 0 over all time) and customers (placed order 1 or more) as separate segments for reporting.
For evergreen campaign sends, combine them into 1 audience.
Use dynamic blocks inside the email to personalise for prospects vs customers instead of splitting the send.
Reserve true audience splits for content that must differ, such as an acquisition discount.

test.method: Compare combined-send revenue against the sum of 2 smaller split sends.

title: Apply spam, bounce and unengaged exclusion segments to every campaign
hypothesis: If every campaign automatically excludes anyone marked spam, hard or repeated soft bounced, or unengaged for 120 to 180 days, then deliverability holds because these campaigns stop sending to profiles that actively hurt sender reputation.

signal.check: Recent campaigns were sent with no exclusion segment attached, or the exclusion list is incomplete.

risk.note: Exclusion setting on future campaigns.

prerequisites: Spam, bounce and unengaged segments built
steps: Build or confirm spam, bounce and unengaged exclusion segments.
Add all 3 as exclusions on the campaign send-setup template.
Confirm the exclusion is applied before every future send.
Recheck after any template change.

test.method: Not a split test; a pre-send checklist item.
test.measure: Whether exclusions are attached on every campaign

title: Require a minimum-sends floor before marking a profile unengaged
hypothesis: If the unengaged segment requires at least 6 emails received in the window before someone counts as unengaged, then the sunset and suppression flows stop wrongly catching new or lightly-emailed subscribers who simply were not sent enough email to react to.

signal.check: The unengaged segment has no minimum-sends condition, so a subscriber who received only 1 or 2 emails already counts as unengaged.

risk.note: Segment condition addition only.

prerequisites: Access to the unengaged segment's condition builder
steps: Open the unengaged segment definition.
Add received at least 6 emails in the same window as the engagement check.
Confirm a recently subscribed test profile with few sends does not qualify as unengaged.

test.method: Not a split test; a segment accuracy check.
test.measure: Unengaged segment size before and after the floor is added

title: Build a VIP segment by order count with a capped extra send and a quarterly offer
hypothesis: If VIP status is defined by 4 or more orders, with at most 1 extra email a month, an entry flow, and a quarterly offer, then top customers feel recognised without being over-emailed, because a clean order-count threshold reads simply as 1 order away from VIP.

signal.check: No VIP segment exists, or VIP customers receive the same treatment and frequency as everyone else.

risk.note: New segment and light-touch treatment.

prerequisites: Order-count and spend distribution
steps: Build a VIP segment for 4 or more orders over all time.
Optionally add a spend-based entry at 3 to 4 times AOV.
Build a short entry flow welcoming VIP status.
Cap VIP-specific extra sends at 1 a month plus a quarterly offer.

test.method: Compare VIP repeat purchase rate and complaint rate before and after the treatment.

title: Build a high-potential segment from recent site activity with no recent order
hypothesis: If a high-potential segment targets people active on site in the last 30 days with 0 orders in that time, and gets 1 to 2 extra emails a month, then conversion rises because these are people already showing interest who just have not converted yet.

signal.check: No segment exists for recently active, non-buying site visitors, so they receive only the standard evergreen cadence.

risk.note: New segment and light extra-send cadence.

prerequisites: Site activity data connected to the email platform
steps: Build a segment for active on site, viewed product, added to cart, or checkout started at least once in the last 30 days.
Add placed order 0 in the last 30 days.
Add 1 to 2 extra targeted emails a month for this segment.
Watch conversion rate for this group specifically.

test.method: Compare conversion rate for the high-potential segment against the standard cadence group.

title: Build a win-back-potential segment for customers 150 to 180 days lapsed
hypothesis: If a win-back-potential segment targets customers who ordered 150 to 180 days ago with nothing in the last 90 days, then a targeted nudge reaches people drifting away before they fully lapse into the standard win-back flow's later stage.

signal.check: No segment exists between the active-customer group and the full win-back flow trigger, so drifting customers get no early nudge.

risk.note: New segment definition using existing order data.

prerequisites: Order history data
steps: Build a segment for placed order at least once in the last 150 to 180 days.
Add placed order 0 in the last 90 days.
Use this segment for a lighter-touch reminder ahead of the full win-back flow.
Track how many convert before reaching the full win-back trigger.

test.method: Compare reorder rate for this segment against customers who skip straight to the full win-back flow.

title: Build buyer-stage segments: non-buyers, first-time, returning, window shoppers, abandoners
hypothesis: If the account has clean segments for non-buyers, first-time buyers, returning buyers, window shoppers, and abandoners without purchase, then campaign and flow targeting improve because each stage's actual behaviour, not just their order count, decides what they receive.

signal.check: The account has no buyer-stage segments beyond a simple has-ordered or has-not-ordered split.

risk.note: New segment set; used for future targeting, not a live change on its own.

prerequisites: Site activity and order history data
steps: Build a non-buyers segment: placed order 0 over all time.
Build first-time (equals 1) and returning (2 or more) segments.
Build a window shoppers segment: 2 or more views or visits in 30 days, 0 orders ever.
Build an abandoners segment: cart or checkout activity in 90 days, 0 orders in 90 days.
Add category-interest and cross-sell segments as needed for the catalogue.

test.method: Not a split test; use these segments in the next round of campaign or flow targeting and compare results.

title: Set a policy for whole-list re-engagement sends after the list is healthy
hypothesis: If a whole-list or near-whole-list re-engagement send goes out at most once a month, only once spam rate is under control and the list is clean, then some openers rejoin the engaged segment without risking the sender's reputation during a fragile period.
does_not_apply_when: The account is mid-repair or spam complaint rate is above the safe target

signal.check: No policy exists for whole-list sends, and one has either never been tried or is being run more than monthly with no health check first.

risk.note: Sending wider raises exposure to inactive profiles; stop if spam or bounce rises.

prerequisites: Spam complaint rate under the safe target
Deliverability repair completed if it was needed
steps: Confirm spam complaint rate is under the safe target and no repair is underway.
Send at most 1 wider re-engagement email a month to all but unsubscribed and suppressed profiles.
Exclude spam marks, bounces and the 180-day unengaged segment even on this wider send.
Stop the practice immediately if spam or bounce rate rises after a send.

test.method: Track spam and bounce rate after each wider send; compare openers who rejoin the engaged segment.
test.read_point: Within 48 hours of each wider send

title: Build location and property segments for country, tags and predictive value
hypothesis: If segments exist for ship-to country, EU vs non-EU, quiz answers, and predictive AOV or lifetime value, then targeting improves because content and offers can match a customer's real geography and predicted value instead of treating the whole list the same.

signal.check: No segments exist beyond basic engagement, so country-specific consent needs and predictive value data go unused.

risk.note: New segment set for targeting.

prerequisites: Ship-to country data
Quiz or predictive data if available
steps: Build ship-to country and EU vs non-EU segments.
Build any location-proximity segments relevant to physical stores.
Build segments from quiz answers or product tags if collected.
Build predictive AOV and lifetime value segments if the platform supports it.

test.method: Not a split test; use these segments for the next round of targeted content.

title: Set a sustainable weekly campaign cadence and never skip a week
hypothesis: If campaign cadence starts at 2 to 3 a week and steps up while unsubscribes, spam and revenue per send hold, and never drops to zero in a week, then email revenue rises because weeks of silence followed by a big sale send read as re-engagement fraud right when the brand most needs inbox placement.

signal.check: The brand sends fewer than 1 campaign some weeks, or sends inconsistently with no set weekly rhythm.

risk.note: Raising cadence too fast can raise unsubscribes; step up gradually and watch the numbers.

prerequisites: Content capacity to sustain a chosen weekly cadence
steps: Set a cadence the team can sustain every week, starting at 2 to 3 campaigns.
Never let a week pass with 0 campaigns.
Step up by 1 send while unsubscribes, spam and revenue per send hold steady.
Cap around 4 to 5 a week unless segments keep each person's total near 3.

test.method: Track unsubscribe, spam and revenue per send at each cadence step before stepping up again.
test.read_point: After 2 to 3 weeks at each cadence level

title: Keep campaign content mostly non-discount
hypothesis: If campaign content stays mostly non-discount, at least 5 non-discount sends per discount send, with at most 1 sale event a month outside the year-end period, then margin holds and open rate stays healthier because the list does not get trained to wait for the next discount.

signal.check: Campaigns lean heavily on discounts, with more than 1 sale event most months or a lower non-discount to discount ratio.

risk.note: Content calendar rebalance.

prerequisites: Campaign calendar with content type tagged
steps: Tag every campaign sent in the last 3 months by type: promotional, product, education, social proof, brand.
Compute the current non-discount to discount ratio.
Rebuild the next month's calendar to keep the ratio at 5 to 1 or better, with at most 1 sale event outside year-end.
Track open rate and unsubscribe rate as the mix shifts.

test.method: Compare open rate, unsubscribe rate and revenue per send before and after rebalancing the mix.

title: Never send 2 consecutive campaigns of the same content type
hypothesis: If no 2 consecutive campaigns share the same content type, alternating education, product, social proof and brand across the week, then engagement holds steadier because the list does not see the same kind of email twice in a row.

signal.check: The last 2 or more campaigns in a row shared the same content type, such as 2 promotional sends back to back.

risk.note: Calendar sequencing rule.

prerequisites: Campaign calendar with content type tagged
steps: Tag every planned campaign by content type.
Check that no 2 in a row share a type.
Follow a sales-focused email with a value-focused email.
Rearrange the calendar wherever 2 consecutive types repeat.

test.method: Not a split test; a calendar-planning rule checked each week.
test.measure: Number of consecutive same-type sends found

title: Rotate through a defined set of non-discount content frameworks
hypothesis: If campaigns rotate through a defined list of frameworks, such as 1 benefit, us vs them, how it is made, product spotlight and reviews, then content planning gets easier and email revenue holds because the calendar always has a ready template instead of defaulting to another promo.

signal.check: Campaign planning starts from scratch each week with no reusable list of content frameworks.

risk.note: Planning tool, not a live change by itself.

prerequisites: Brand content and product information to fill each framework
steps: Write a reference list of content frameworks: 1 benefit, 1 feature, FAQ, how it is made, how to use, back in stock, reviews, us vs them, myth vs fact, blog promo, research study, product spotlight, launch sequence.
Assign a framework to each open slot in the campaign calendar.
Cap obscure-holiday content at 1 to 2 a month.
Refresh the framework list quarterly with what performed best.

test.method: Not a split test; track click rate by framework used over time.

title: Write each campaign around 1 micro-topic and 1 takeaway
hypothesis: If each campaign is built around 1 specific micro-topic, such as why we use a particular ingredient, instead of a broad theme like our product is amazing, then engagement rises because a specific angle is more interesting and easier to act on than a general claim.

signal.check: Recent campaigns cover broad, generic themes with no specific micro-topic or takeaway.

risk.note: Copy planning approach, not a structural change.

prerequisites: Brand's niche, macro topics and product details
steps: Start from the brand's niche and list macro topics within it.
Break each macro topic into specific micro-topics.
Pick 1 micro-topic per campaign and write toward its 1 takeaway.
Avoid combining more than 1 topic in a single send.

test.method: Compare click rate on micro-topic campaigns against broad-theme campaigns.
test.read_point: After 4 to 6 campaigns of each type

title: Structure every campaign to walk from problem to process to product
hypothesis: If every campaign teaches the problem, then the process, then places the product as the solution, then click-through to product pages rises because the email builds a reason to buy instead of jumping straight to a pitch.

signal.check: Recent campaigns open directly with a product pitch with no problem or process framing first.

risk.note: Copy structure change only.

prerequisites: Existing campaign copy templates
steps: Open with the problem the customer actually has.
Walk through the process or reasoning that leads to a solution.
Place the product as the answer, with a clear path to buy.
Review recent campaigns against this structure and rewrite any that skip straight to the pitch.

test.method: Compare click-through to product pages before and after applying the structure.

title: Build the campaign calendar with a repeatable, staged method
hypothesis: If the campaign calendar is built by locking fixed dates first, then adding awareness days, then seasonal content, then micro-topic fill, then checking the mix, and staying 2 weeks ahead, then planning time drops and gaps stop appearing because the method covers every slot in a fixed order.

signal.check: The calendar is built week by week with no repeatable method, and content is often written the day before it sends.

risk.note: Planning process, not a live send change.

prerequisites: A shared calendar tool
steps: Lock fixed dates: launches, real restocks, planned sales, milestones.
Add 1 to 2 fitting awareness days.
Map existing content to the season.
Fill remaining slots with micro-topics from the framework list.
Run the mix check against the content-mix target.
Keep the calendar 2 weeks ahead of send date at all times.
Review at month end for 20 to 30 minutes and feed patterns into next month.

test.method: Not a split test; track whether the calendar stays 2 weeks ahead over successive months.
test.measure: Days ahead of send that content is finalised

title: Use campaigns as a fast test lab, then port winners into flows
hypothesis: If a winning campaign angle, such as an education email or a returns-policy explainer, gets ported into the matching flow, then flow performance rises because campaigns give feedback in 24 hours while flows take longer to read, so campaigns are a faster place to find what works first.

signal.check: Strong-performing campaign angles have never been checked against flow content for a matching opportunity.

risk.note: Content reuse; flows can be reverted if the port underperforms.

prerequisites: Campaign performance history by angle
steps: Identify the top-performing campaign angle from the last quarter.
Find the matching flow, such as welcome, cart or post-purchase.
Adapt the winning angle into that flow's content, adding the flow's relevant code or context.
Track the flow's performance after the port.

test.method: Compare the flow email's performance before and after porting the winning campaign angle.
test.measure: other:revenue_per_recipient on the updated flow email

title: Reserve resend-to-non-openers for launches, restocks and sale-closers only
hypothesis: If resending to non-openers with a new subject line is reserved for launches, real restocks and a sale's last day, then it stays effective because using it on every evergreen send would train the list to ignore the first send.

signal.check: Resend to non-openers is used on routine evergreen campaigns with no real time pressure.

risk.note: Usage discipline, not a structural change.

prerequisites: Resend or sequence-builder function available
steps: Reserve resends for launch day, a real restock, or a sale's last day only.
Write a genuinely new subject line for the resend, not a repeat.
Wait a minimum of 48 hours before resending.
Narrow the resend audience to true non-openers of the original send.

test.method: Compare resend click rate on reserved-use sends against past overuse on evergreen sends.

title: Write every email for a 3 to 5 second skim
hypothesis: If every email is written for a 3 to 5 second skim with bold points, short sections and a word-count ceiling, then click-through rises because a shopper reading one-handed while comparing tabs needs the first line to survive that split attention.

signal.check: Recent emails run long paragraphs with no bolding or clear skim points, over 300 words for a campaign or over 100 for a welcome email.

risk.note: Copy editing pass only.

prerequisites: Existing email copy
steps: Bold the key point in each section.
Cut paragraphs to short sections, aiming for 1 to 2 mobile scrolls.
Cap campaigns at 100 to 300 words and welcome emails under 100.
Read the draft aloud and cut anything that does not survive a 3 to 5 second skim.

test.method: Compare click-through rate before and after applying the skim-friendly rewrite.

title: Write email copy at a simple, tenth-grade or below reading level
hypothesis: If email copy uses simple words in active voice at a reading level someone deciding fast can follow, then click-through rises because the shopper is quickly judging whether the product solves their problem, not reading carefully.

signal.check: Recent email copy uses complex sentences, jargon or passive voice.

risk.note: Copy editing pass only.

prerequisites: Existing email copy
steps: Read each draft aloud and cut 20 to 30 percent of the words.
Rewrite passive sentences as active.
Replace jargon or complex words with simpler alternatives.
Check reading level against a tenth-grade ceiling before sending.

test.method: Compare click-through rate before and after the simplification pass.

title: Lead every email with a pain or outcome headline, not a feature
hypothesis: If the headline names the pain or the outcome instead of a product feature, then open-to-click rate rises because a benefit or outcome headline hooks interest faster than a feature statement does.

signal.check: Recent email headlines lead with a feature or product name instead of a pain point or outcome.

risk.note: Headline rewrite only.

prerequisites: List of the product's real pain points and outcomes
steps: List the top pain points or outcomes the product addresses.
Rewrite the headline to name 1 of them directly.
Follow with 1 to 2 supporting sentences, then the first button.
Avoid leading with a feature name or product spec.

test.method: A/B test a pain or outcome headline against the current feature-led headline.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, about 2 weeks

title: Run a defined research routine before writing any new email angle
hypothesis: If every new angle starts with 2 to 4 hours of research across the Ad Library, recent Amazon reviews, podcasts and the brand's own support tickets and reviews, then copy converts better because it reflects real objections and language instead of guessing.

signal.check: New angles are written from the copywriter's own assumptions with no research step logged.

risk.note: Research process; no live change by itself.

prerequisites: Access to the Ad Library, review platforms, and the brand's own support and social channels
steps: Pull audience demographics from analytics as a baseline.
Search the Ad Library for the category and note competitor angles, treating them as signals only.
Read recent Amazon and Trustpilot reviews for the category, filtered to most recent, and log objections and praise.
Check podcasts, thought leaders and comment sections for language and objections, verifying any study before quoting it.
Review the brand's own Instagram language, blog, support tickets and reviews tagged by objection.
Write a short research doc with angles, benefits, objections and the brand's proof for each before drafting copy.

test.method: Compare click-through and placed order rate of researched angles against non-researched angles.
test.read_point: After each new angle's first send

title: Sell on at most 3 points and use reviews that each answer 1 objection
hypothesis: If an email sells on at most 3 points and pairs each proof element with 1 named objection, then conversion rises because a focused pitch is easier to act on than a long list of features.

signal.check: A recent email lists more than 3 selling points, or uses reviews with no specific objection attached.

risk.note: Copy editing pass only.

prerequisites: Reviews tagged by objection
steps: Pick the 3 strongest selling points for the angle.
Cut any additional points from the draft.
Pair each point, where relevant, with a review naming that specific objection.
Avoid a face next to a sensitive topic.

test.method: Compare conversion rate of the focused version against a longer, unfocused draft.

title: Reserve insecurity-anchor copy for angles the brand voice allows and the cause is true
hypothesis: If deep emotional or insecurity-anchor copy is used only where the brand voice allows it and any external cause named is true and provable, then trust holds because the brand never blames the customer or invents an external villain to sell a product.

signal.check: A draft uses an insecurity angle, blames the customer, or names an external cause with no evidence behind it.

risk.note: Getting this wrong risks brand trust; check against brand voice limits first.

prerequisites: Brand voice limits on fear or insecurity angles
steps: Check the brand's stated voice limits before drafting an insecurity-anchor angle.
If used, confirm any external cause named is true and provable, never blaming the customer.
Never name a competitor company directly.
Use icon-row perk copy instead for lighter, non-emotional benefits.

test.method: Not a split test; a content review gate before send.
test.measure: Whether the angle passes the brand-voice and honesty check

title: Check every claim against the brand record before an email ships
hypothesis: If every regulated or factual claim is checked against the brand's spec sheet or returns data before send, and never implied to dodge the rule, then the brand avoids a false claim reaching a customer or a regulator.

signal.check: A draft states or implies a claim about ingredients, materials, safety or shipping speed with no check against the brand record.

risk.note: An unsupported claim can create legal exposure once sent; verify before every send.

prerequisites: Brand record of approved claims, guarantees, shipping times and returns policy
steps: List every claim in the draft, including implied ones.
Check each against the brand's approved claims, guarantees, shipping times and returns policy.
Remove or rewrite any claim the brand record does not support.
Check current market rules on implied claims before using ambiguous wording.

test.method: Not a split test; a mandatory check before every send.
test.measure: Whether every claim in the draft matches the brand record

title: Write short, curiosity-driven subject lines with hand-written preview text
hypothesis: If subject lines are short with a real curiosity gap or value stated up front, and preview text is written by hand to extend the subject, then click-through rises because the reader gets a reason to open beyond a generic default preview.

signal.check: Subject lines oversell the product, run long, or leave the default preview text unedited.

risk.note: Copy change only.

prerequisites: Existing subject line and preview text
steps: Keep the subject short, under about 50 characters, with value in the first few words.
Frame a curiosity gap around a real product benefit, restock, or deadline, never an oversell.
Write the preview text by hand to add a second reason, not repeat the subject.
Never write a subject that promises something the email does not deliver.

test.method: A/B test 2 subject line options, judged on placed order rate not opens.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch, for flow emails; 5 to 10 campaigns for campaign subject tests

title: Keep 1 consistent sender identity across flows and campaigns
hypothesis: If the sender name and email stay consistent across flows and campaigns, on the authenticated domain with reply-to at support, then trust holds because a customer recognises the same sender identity from their cart email through to a win-back email months later.

signal.check: Different flows or campaigns use different sender names or emails with no consistent identity.

risk.note: Sender setting change; test founder vs brand name before locking it in.

prerequisites: Authenticated sending domain
Support inbox for reply-to
steps: Pick either the brand name or founder plus brand as the sender identity.
Set the sender email on the authenticated domain with reply-to at support.
Apply the same identity across every flow and campaign.
Test founder vs brand name once, then keep the winner consistent.

test.method: A/B test founder vs brand sender name on a campaign, then apply the winner everywhere.
test.read_point: After 3 to 4 campaigns per sender variant

title: Treat AI-drafted email copy as a draft only, never as final
hypothesis: If AI drafts are primed with brand, product, audience and voice details, then stripped of generic AI tells and fact-checked before use, then email quality holds because the model's default output tends toward generic language and can invent claims.

signal.check: An AI-drafted email ships with generic AI-sounding phrases, no fact-check, or a missing CTA.

risk.note: Unedited AI claims can create trust and compliance risk; always fact-check before send.

prerequisites: Brand, product, audience and voice reference material for prompting
steps: Prime the AI prompt with brand, products, audience, voice and USPs.
Ask for a headline, sub-headline and 2 to 3 sentences, not a full finished email.
Strip generic AI tells such as crafting, enthusiasts, unleash.
Write product blurbs yourself rather than relying on the draft.
Fact-check every claim against the brand record and add any missing CTA.

test.method: Not a split test; a mandatory editing checklist before any AI-assisted draft ships.
test.measure: Whether the draft passes the fact-check and AI-tell removal steps

title: Build emails at 600px wide with mobile-legible text sizes
hypothesis: If emails are built at about 600px wide with 18px desktop and at least 16px mobile text and 1.5 line height, then readability rises because most orders come from a phone screen and small text on that screen is the first thing that loses the reader.

signal.check: Recent emails use text under 16px on mobile, tight line height, or a width that does not render cleanly on common phone screens.

risk.note: Template sizing fix only.

prerequisites: Access to the email template's base styles
steps: Set the template width to about 600px.
Set desktop body text to 18px and mobile to at least 16px.
Set line height to about 1.5.
Set block padding around 20px between sections.

test.method: Not a split test; a rendering check on a real phone and desktop preview.
test.measure: Whether text is legible without zooming on mobile
test.read_point: Before every send, as part of the test-send checklist

title: Put the headline, a short line, a big button and the code above the fold
hypothesis: If the headline, 1 to 2 sentences, a big button and, for promos, the code all sit above the fold, then click-through rises because the large majority of readers never scroll further.

signal.check: The first button or the discount code sits below the first screen's worth of content.

risk.note: Layout reorder only.

prerequisites: Existing email template
steps: Move the headline, 1 to 2 sentences and the first CTA button above the fold.
For promotional emails, bold the code and place it above the fold too.
Check the layout on a common phone screen size, not just desktop.
Cut anything competing for space above the fold that is not essential.

test.method: Compare click-through rate before and after moving key elements above the fold.

title: End every section on a path to a product page, 1 decision per email
hypothesis: If every section ends with a CTA to a product page or the cart, never a generic learn more, and the whole email drives 1 decision, then click-through rises because the goal is a purchase path, not just engagement.

signal.check: A recent email has multiple competing CTAs, or ends a section with a generic learn more link instead of a product path.

risk.note: Layout and link fix only.

prerequisites: Existing email template
steps: Add a CTA button at the end of every section and under every product.
Point every CTA at a product or cart page, never a generic learn more.
Confirm the whole email drives toward 1 decision, even if it shows several buttons.
End with a shop all or shop bestsellers CTA.

test.method: Compare click-through rate before and after tightening CTA consistency.

title: Cap product blocks at 3 to 5 items per email
hypothesis: If product-focused emails show 3 to 5 products, laid out 1 per row with copy or as a 2x2 grid, never a 3x2 grid on mobile, then click-through rises because the layout stays scannable instead of overwhelming the reader.

signal.check: A recent email shows more than 5 products or uses a 3x2 grid on mobile.

risk.note: Layout change only.

prerequisites: Existing product-block template
steps: Cut the product count to 3 to 5 per email.
Use 1 product per row with copy, or a 2x2 grid.
Never use a 3x2 grid on mobile.
Preview on mobile to confirm the grid renders as intended.

test.method: Compare click-through rate before and after resizing the product block.

title: Replace paragraph explanations with infographics
hypothesis: If emails use checklists, icon rows, comparison tables or timelines instead of paragraphs to explain how a product works, then engagement rises because a visual explains a before-and-after or a process faster than text alone.

signal.check: Emails explaining how a product works or comparing it to alternatives rely on paragraph text instead of a visual format.

risk.note: Design build for existing content.

prerequisites: Design resource able to build simple infographics
steps: Identify any email explaining a process, comparison or before-and-after in paragraph form.
Convert it into a checklist, icon row, comparison table or timeline.
Use icons instead of bullets throughout.
Aim for at least 1 infographic-style element per campaign where relevant.

test.method: Compare engagement on the infographic version against the paragraph version.

title: Vary layout and imagery between sends and match the brand's real look
hypothesis: If layout, imagery and theme vary between sends and match the brand's actual site and Instagram look, using real product photos where accuracy matters, then trust and engagement hold because the same template every time reads as stale, and mismatched studio photos feel off-brand.

signal.check: Every recent email uses the same template and layout, or uses studio photos that look nothing like the brand's own Instagram content.

risk.note: Design variation within brand guidelines.

prerequisites: Real product photos
Brand's current site and Instagram look for reference
steps: Review the last 5 to 10 sends for layout repetition.
Build 2 to 3 alternate layout templates within the brand's style.
Use real product photos wherever accuracy matters, matching the brand's actual site and Instagram look.
Rotate templates so no 2 consecutive sends look identical.

test.method: Not a split test; track engagement across template variants over time.
test.read_point: After a full rotation of templates

title: Give every image alt text with the offer, a deep link and compression
hypothesis: If every image gets alt text carrying the offer, links to the specific product or collection page rather than the homepage, and is compressed, then click-through and load speed both improve because images-off readers and slow connections still get a usable email.

signal.check: Images are missing alt text, link to the homepage instead of a specific page, or are uncompressed multi-megabyte files.

risk.note: Content and file fix within existing templates.

prerequisites: Image compression tool
steps: Add alt text to every image, including the offer text where relevant.
Link each image and button to the specific product or collection page, never the homepage.
Compress every slice through a compression tool.
Confirm only 1 link per image slice.

test.method: Not a split test; a pre-send checklist item, with click-through tracked over time.
test.measure: email_click_rate, page_weight_kb of the sent email

title: Keep the offer, product names and footer as live text, not locked inside images
hypothesis: If the offer, product names and footer are built as live text rather than baked into images, then the email reads correctly for inbox AI features and with images off, because an image-only email otherwise reads as empty.

signal.check: Viewing the email with images turned off shows a mostly blank message, with the offer, product names or footer missing.

risk.note: Template rebuild to add live text blocks.

prerequisites: Email builder support for live text and native product blocks
steps: Identify which parts of the template are currently baked into images: offer bar, product names, footer.
Rebuild those as live text blocks or native product blocks.
View the email with images off and confirm the offer, products and footer still read.
Keep a live top bar and live footer with category links.

test.method: Not a split test; a rendering check with images off.
test.measure: Whether the offer and footer read correctly with images disabled

title: Build a standard footer with unsubscribe, address, category links and trust icons
hypothesis: If every email uses a standard footer with a mandatory unsubscribe link, organisation name and address via dynamic tags, category links and trust icons, then compliance holds and a small amount of extra navigation revenue is captured from footer clicks.

signal.check: The footer is missing the organisation address, has no category links, or was built manually per email instead of as a saved universal block.

risk.note: Template build; keeps the mandatory unsubscribe link.

prerequisites: Organisation address and category link list
steps: Build a footer with unsubscribe, organisation name and address via dynamic tags, category links, trust icons and social icons.
Save it as a universal block.
Apply it to every template.
Recheck after any platform update that changing dynamic tags might affect.

test.method: Not a split test; a compliance and completeness check.
test.measure: Whether every send uses the standard footer

title: Test-send every email to yourself on desktop and mobile before scheduling
hypothesis: If every email is test-sent and every link is clicked on both desktop and mobile before scheduling, then broken links and rendering issues stop reaching customers because the fix happens before the send, not after.

signal.check: Emails are scheduled directly from the builder with no test send and link check step.

risk.note: Quality check step, catches issues before they ship.

prerequisites: Ability to send a test email to yourself
steps: Send a test email to yourself before every schedule.
Click every link on both a phone and a desktop.
Check for rendering issues, odd padding or broken images.
Only schedule the send once the test passes.

test.method: Not a split test; a mandatory pre-send step.
test.measure: Number of broken links or rendering issues caught before send

title: Build emails as compressed slices plus live text, not 1 giant image
hypothesis: If emails are built from a copy-first layout, sliced into 1 image per link target and compressed, with short text rebuilt as live text in the platform, then load speed and click-through both improve because no single giant image slows the email or hides its content from images-off readers.

signal.check: An email is built as 1 large image, or slices are uncompressed and unusually large in file size.

expected_effect.size: unknown, 1 source demo showed about 35 KB total

risk.note: Build process change within existing design tools.

prerequisites: A design tool such as Figma
Image compression tool
steps: Lay out the email copy first, 1 section per row, before designing.
Design each section at 600px wide in the design tool.
Slice 1 image per link target, never 1 giant image, and export at 2x.
Compress every slice in a batch tool.
Rebuild short text, such as headline, code and footer, as live text in the email platform instead of leaving it in the image.

test.method: Check total email file size against the platform's clipping threshold before every send.

title: Fix content quality before chasing technical deliverability fixes
hypothesis: If content quality, real bestsellers, real photos, a real founder voice and reply invitations, is fixed before chasing technical settings, then deliverability improves faster because sender reputation is built mostly from engagement, not just authentication.

signal.check: A deliverability problem is being treated purely as a technical issue, with no review of content quality, variety or real value.

risk.note: Content review; complements, not replaces, technical fixes.

prerequisites: Recent send history to review for content quality
steps: Review the last several sends for varied topics and layouts.
Confirm a real bestseller, a real product photo and a real founder voice are being used, not generic stock content.
Confirm 1 clear above-the-fold CTA and category footer links exist.
Invite replies with copy such as ask us anything.
Only after this review, move to technical deliverability fixes such as domain authentication.

test.method: Track open rate, Apple opens excluded, before and after the content quality pass.

title: Run a staged deliverability repair ladder when sender reputation degrades
hypothesis: If a degraded sender restricts sends to a narrow engaged segment and widens step by step only as open rate holds above 50 percent, then deliverability recovers because the sender rebuilds a track record with the audience most likely to engage before expanding.
does_not_apply_when: Opens, Apple opens excluded, are already healthy on engaged sends and no placement problem is showing

signal.check: Open rate on engaged sends, Apple opens excluded, is under about 30 to 40 percent, or a placement test shows heavy spam or promotions folder placement.

expected_effect.size: toward 45 to 50 percent or higher on engaged sends

risk.note: Temporarily reduces reach; step back down a stage if opens fall at any point.

prerequisites: Engaged segments at 14, 30, 60 and 90 days built
Domain authentication complete
steps: Diagnose using the last 5 campaigns' deliverability tab and a placement test.
Improve email content quality first.
Pause all flows except welcome, browse, cart, checkout and post-purchase.
Send 3 strong campaigns a week to the 14-day engaged segment only.
After 2 weeks or 3 straight sends at 50 percent or higher opens, widen to 30 days.
Repeat the gate at 60, then 90 days, turning all flows back on once 90 days is stable.
Step back down 1 stage and hold 2 more weeks if opens fall at any point.

test.method: Track open rate, Apple opens excluded, at each stage before widening further.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 3 sends at each stage

title: Reserve SMS for high-urgency, low-frequency news only
hypothesis: If SMS carries only launches, real restocks, sales and big news, while nurture and evergreen content stay in email, then SMS unsubscribe rate stays lower because testimonials and brand stories by text raised unsubscribes and gave poor return in tested accounts.

signal.check: Recent SMS sends include testimonials, brand story content or evergreen bestseller pushes instead of urgent, time-bound news.

risk.note: Content policy change only.

prerequisites: SMS platform live
steps: Review the last 10 SMS sends for content type.
Move any nurture, brand-story or evergreen content back to email only.
Reserve SMS for launches, drops, real restocks, sales, flash sales, exclusive offers and big news.
Track SMS unsubscribe rate after the policy change.

test.method: Compare SMS unsubscribe rate before and after limiting content to urgent news.

title: Collect explicit SMS consent and keep opt-out handling on every program
hypothesis: If SMS consent is confirmed explicit before any send and STOP-style opt-out handling stays on every program including iMessage, then legal exposure drops because texting without consent or removing opt-out handling is a real compliance risk, not just a style choice.

signal.check: Any SMS or business-messaging program lacks confirmed explicit consent, or opt-out handling has been shortened or removed.

risk.note: Removing opt-out handling is a compliance risk in most markets; keep it regardless of the messaging channel.

prerequisites: SMS consent records
Web check on opt-out requirements per market
steps: Audit every SMS or business-messaging segment for confirmed explicit consent.
Confirm STOP or the local equivalent opt-out works on every channel, including iMessage.
Never shorten opt-out language to save characters if it breaks the required disclosure.
Recheck after adding any new messaging channel.

test.method: Not a split test; a compliance audit.
test.measure: Share of SMS sends with confirmed opt-out handling active
test.read_point: Before launching any new messaging channel

title: Set SMS quiet hours to the strictest legal window for each recipient's location
hypothesis: If SMS quiet hours are set to the strictest legal window for the recipient's actual country and state, in their local time, then the brand avoids sending outside a legally protected window that varies by market.

signal.check: SMS quiet hours use 1 fixed window for the whole list regardless of the recipient's country or state, or the window has never been checked against current law.

risk.note: Sending outside legal quiet hours can carry fines; check current law per market before setting the window.

prerequisites: Web check on legal quiet hours per country and US state
steps: Check current legal quiet hours for every country and state the brand texts.
Set the platform's quiet-hours setting to the strictest applicable window, in recipient local time.
For India, check the TRAI promotional time window specifically.
Recheck this before expanding SMS into any new market.

test.method: Not a split test; confirm no test sends land outside the configured quiet hours.
test.measure: Whether any send was scheduled inside quiet hours and held
test.read_point: Before every SMS send, and before expanding to a new market

title: Start SMS send windows around midday, test later slots
hypothesis: If SMS campaigns default to sending between 11am and 2 or 3pm local time, with last-chance texts by early evening, then click and revenue rise because this window matches when most sources report the best response on their own data.

signal.check: SMS sends go out early morning, late at night, or with no consistent send-time policy.

risk.note: Scheduling change only, within quiet-hour limits.

prerequisites: Quiet hours already configured
steps: Default SMS campaign sends to 11am to 2 or 3pm recipient local time.
Test a later window, 4 to 5pm, against the default.
Schedule last-chance texts by 6 to 7pm.
Track clicks and revenue by hour on the brand's own sends and adjust.

test.method: Compare click and revenue by send hour across several campaigns.

title: Start SMS cadence conservatively and only raise it through a proven holdout
hypothesis: If SMS cadence starts at about 1 real-news send a week and only steps up through a holdout test that watches unsubscribes, then SMS revenue grows without a spike in unsubscribes, because cadence set by fear or by vendor advice tends to run either too low or too aggressively.

signal.check: SMS cadence was set by a vendor's recommendation or gut feel, with no holdout test behind any increase.

risk.note: Raising cadence without a holdout risks an unsubscribe spike.

prerequisites: SMS holdout test capability (see the SMS holdout idea)
steps: Start SMS campaign cadence at about 1 real-news send a week.
Never raise cadence without a holdout test that compares revenue per subscriber against unsubscribe rate.
Never send campaign texts to active subscription customers.
Step up 1 message at a time and stop at the first rise in unsubscribes.

test.method: Run the SMS holdout test method before each cadence increase.

title: Adjust SMS frequency by the product's purchase cycle and buyer state
hypothesis: If SMS frequency is set by the product's real purchase cycle, lower for a slow-cycle category and zero campaign texts to active subscription customers, then unsubscribe rate stays lower because the cadence matches how often the customer actually thinks about buying again.

signal.check: SMS cadence is 1 fixed rate for the whole list regardless of product purchase cycle or subscription status.

risk.note: Segment-based cadence adjustment.

prerequisites: Repeat purchase interval and subscription status per customer
steps: Pull the typical purchase cycle for the brand's main categories.
Lower campaign frequency for long-cycle products.
Exclude active subscription customers from campaign texts entirely.
Recheck the segment quarterly as purchase behaviour shifts.

test.method: Compare unsubscribe rate across cadence tiers matched to purchase cycle.

title: Keep every SMS to 1 message segment and check the platform's counter
hypothesis: If every SMS stays within 1 segment, 160 GSM-7 characters or 70 with any emoji or Unicode character, checked against the platform's own counter, then SMS cost per send stays predictable because going over 1 segment silently doubles or triples the cost of that message.

signal.check: Recent SMS drafts include an emoji or special character with no check of the resulting segment count.

risk.note: Copy check before send.

prerequisites: Access to the platform's segment counter
steps: Draft the SMS copy including the opt-out text and any link.
Check the platform's segment counter before sending.
Cut characters or remove emoji if the message exceeds 1 segment.
Confirm the segment count and cost per recipient before scheduling.

test.method: Not a split test; a pre-send cost check.

title: Reserve MMS for sends where the image proves a net profit gain
hypothesis: If MMS is only used where a tested image send shows a real net profit gain after its 2 to 3 times higher cost, then SMS program margin holds because MMS is not used out of habit on sends where a plain text message performs just as well.

signal.check: MMS is used as the default format for SMS campaigns with no net-profit comparison against plain text on record.

risk.note: Testing MMS costs more per send during the test period.

prerequisites: Cost per SMS and MMS segment on the brand's plan
steps: Pick a send type to test, such as a launch or a new product reveal.
Run an MMS version against a plain-text version to a comparable audience.
Compute net profit, revenue minus the extra send cost, for each version.
Reserve MMS going forward only for send types that proved a net-profit gain.

test.method: Compare net profit per send between MMS and plain text on matched sends.

title: Capture phone numbers as an activate-the-offer step after email
hypothesis: If the phone step frames itself as finishing or activating the already-promised offer rather than a new signup, with no extra discount by default, then phone submit rate rises because the copy asks for 1 more small step to unlock something already earned.

signal.check: The phone-capture step says continue or sign up for texts, or offers a separate discount just for the phone number.

expected_effect.size: toward about 15 percent of form viewers with a quiz-first form

risk.note: Copy and button change only.

prerequisites: Email step already collecting the full offer
steps: Show the full offer in the email step.
Write the phone step as finish signing up with text to activate the offer.
Change the button from continue to claim now.
By default, do not add an extra discount for the phone number; test a bigger SMS offer only if phone submits stay under 10 percent.

test.method: Track phone submit rate by device after the copy change.

title: Build a 2 to 3 text SMS welcome sequence inside about 5 days
hypothesis: If the SMS welcome sends the code immediately, a differentiator reminder 2 to 3 days later, and a last-chance text by day 5, then SMS welcome conversion rises because the sequence stays short and each text has 1 clear job.

signal.check: No SMS welcome sequence exists, or it spreads over more than a week with no clear structure.

risk.note: New flow build.

prerequisites: SMS platform live
Phone-capture step built
steps: Text 1, immediate: welcome plus a short brand remark, with the code and a link.
Text 2, 2 days later: 1 differentiator plus a code reminder.
Text 3, 2 days later: the offer expires soon, only if it truly does.
Optional text 4: any questions I can answer.
Add a filter: placed order 0 since starting this flow.

test.method: Track SMS welcome conversion rate after launch.

title: Send exactly 1 abandonment SMS per flow, within 48 hours, split by buyer status
hypothesis: If each abandonment flow sends only 1 SMS within 48 hours of the event, with non-buyers getting the welcome code and buyers a plain reminder, then SMS unsubscribe rate stays lower because multiple texts per abandonment event are the fastest way to trigger a complaint.

signal.check: An abandonment flow sends more than 1 SMS, or sends the same message to both buyers and non-buyers.

risk.note: SMS step addition to existing email abandonment flows.

prerequisites: SMS consent list
Email abandonment flows already built
steps: Add a single SMS step to each abandonment flow: browse after about 60 minutes, cart and checkout after 1 to 2 hours.
Filter to has SMS consent.
Split by placed order at least once: non-buyers get the welcome code reminder, buyers get a plain reminder with no code.
Confirm the platform enforces or is configured for only 1 SMS per person per flow within 48 hours.

test.method: Track SMS unsubscribe rate on abandonment flows after the change.

title: Send 1 post-purchase SMS around day 10 to 14 with no offer
