hypothesis: If a single post-purchase SMS asks how the product is going a few days after delivery, with no offer, plus a separate replenishment text timed to supply, then SMS complaint rate stays low because buyers are not asked to buy again right after their last purchase.

signal.check: No post-purchase SMS exists, or it includes a discount offer immediately after the sale.

risk.note: New SMS step.

prerequisites: SMS consent list
Delivery time estimate
steps: Send 1 text around day 10 to 14, a few days after expected delivery.
Ask a simple are you liking it question, with an optional soft cross-sell link.
Include no discount offer at this stage.
Build a separate replenishment text timed to days of supply plus delivery minus a few days.

test.method: Track click and unsubscribe rate on the post-purchase SMS after launch.

title: Set SMS win-back at 60 to 90 days with a short flash offer
hypothesis: If SMS win-back triggers at 60 to 90 days or twice the average purchase interval, with a 72-hour flash offer then a last-chance text 2 days later, then a lapsed customer gets 1 clear, time-bound reason to return by text instead of a vague reminder.

signal.check: No SMS win-back exists, or it fires on a fixed schedule unrelated to the brand's own purchase interval.

risk.note: New SMS flow step.

prerequisites: Average purchase interval
SMS consent list
steps: Set the trigger at 60 to 90 days, or twice the average purchase interval, whichever fits the product.
Text 1: flash offer with a 72-hour deadline.
Text 2, 2 days later: last chance.
Confirm the offer is a unique or genuinely expiring code.

test.method: Track win-back conversion rate from the SMS flow after launch.

title: Decide the SMS audience policy from click and unsubscribe trend, not habit
hypothesis: If the SMS audience policy, broadcast with light exclusion versus a tighter engaged segment, is chosen based on the current click and unsubscribe trend rather than habit, then SMS revenue and list health both hold because the policy matches what the data is actually saying right now.

signal.check: The SMS audience policy has never been revisited even as click rate fell under 5 percent or unsubscribe rate rose above 1 percent.

risk.note: Audience policy adjustment only.

prerequisites: SMS click and unsubscribe trend data
steps: Track SMS click rate and unsubscribe rate over the last 3 to 6 sends.
If click rate falls under about 5 percent or unsubscribes exceed about 1 percent, tighten to an engaged SMS segment.
If both stay healthy, a broadcast with light exclusion, such as high-volume 0-click profiles, can continue.
Recheck this decision every quarter or after any cadence change.

test.method: Compare click and unsubscribe rate on the broadcast policy against the tightened segment policy.
test.read_point: After each policy change, over 3 to 4 sends

title: Track SMS on click rate, unsubscribe rate, delivery rate and net profit
hypothesis: If SMS performance is judged on click rate, unsubscribe rate, delivery rate and net profit per send instead of open rate, then decisions get more accurate because open rate is not a reliable SMS metric and inflated open-rate claims can hide a program that is actually losing money.

signal.check: SMS reporting leads with an open-rate figure, or net profit per send is never computed.

expected_effect.size: click rate target 5 to 15 percent, unsubscribe under 1 percent, delivery over 90 percent

risk.note: Reporting change only.

prerequisites: Per-send cost data to compute net profit
steps: Drop open rate from the SMS reporting dashboard.
Track click rate, unsubscribe rate and delivery rate per send.
Compute net profit per send: revenue minus segment cost times recipients, in code.
Set targets: click 5 to 15 percent, unsubscribe under 1 percent, delivery over 90 percent.

test.method: Not a split test; a reporting and target-setting change tracked over time.

title: Run an SMS holdout test once SMS spend passes a real threshold
hypothesis: If a 3-cell holdout, normal cadence, no messages, and double cadence, runs once SMS spend is meaningful, then true incremental SMS revenue is known because comparing against a true no-message cell separates real lift from revenue the brand would have earned anyway.

signal.check: SMS spend has grown to a meaningful monthly cost with no holdout ever run to prove incremental revenue.

risk.note: A no-message cell temporarily reduces revenue from that group, by design.

prerequisites: Enough SMS list size to split into meaningful cells
Baseline revenue per subscriber
steps: Compute baseline messages per subscriber per month, revenue per message, and unsubscribe rate.
Randomise SMS subscribers into 3 cells: 50 percent current cadence, 25 percent no campaign texts, 25 percent double cadence.
Keep flows running for all cells; only campaign cadence changes.
Run long enough to read revenue given the brand's own weekly revenue per subscriber.
Compare revenue per subscriber in each cell against the no-message cell, subtracting message cost, in code.

test.method: The holdout test itself is the test; read results after the sizing period.
test.read_point: After a period long enough to read revenue per subscriber reliably, sized from the brand's own data

title: Pick 1 email and SMS sequencing pattern for abandonment and hold it
hypothesis: If 1 chosen pattern, such as email at 30 minutes then 1 SMS at 1 to 2 hours if no order, is held consistently instead of switching between patterns, then results become readable because a stable pattern can actually be tested against an alternative.

signal.check: Email and SMS sequencing for the same abandonment event changes from send to send with no fixed pattern.

risk.note: Sequencing policy change only.

prerequisites: Both email and SMS abandonment flows built
steps: Pick 1 pattern for cart and checkout: email at 30 minutes, then 1 SMS at 1 to 2 hours if no order.
For campaigns and launches, pick email first then SMS 5 to 6 hours later, or the reverse.
Hold the chosen pattern for the full test period before switching.
Test the alternative pattern only as a deliberate experiment, not an ad hoc change.

test.method: A/B test the chosen pattern against 1 alternative, read on net profit.
test.read_point: After a full test period, at least 2 weeks

title: Start conversational SMS with 1 reply-inviting question in an existing flow
hypothesis: If a single flow adds a question such as any questions I can answer, and replies are staffed and objections get tagged into flows and product pages, then conversion rises for long-consideration or high-ticket products because a real 2-way conversation resolves doubts that a 1-way message cannot.
does_not_apply_when: The team has no capacity to staff SMS replies within a reasonable time

signal.check: SMS is entirely 1-way with no reply-inviting question anywhere in the flows, on a high-consideration or high-ticket product.

risk.note: Requires real staff capacity to answer replies promptly.

prerequisites: A team member or process able to answer SMS replies quickly
steps: Confirm who will answer replies and how fast.
Add a question to the last welcome or abandonment text: do you have any questions I can answer.
Staff the reply queue and tag objections that come in.
Feed common objections back into flows and product page copy.

test.method: Track reply rate and conversion rate for recipients who engaged in a reply exchange.

title: Pilot RCS or iMessage business messaging as a holdout, not a default rollout
hypothesis: If RCS or iMessage business messaging is piloted with a holdout and creative held constant, judged after its higher cost, then the brand avoids overpaying for a novelty lift that fades, especially in markets where iPhone share is low.
does_not_apply_when: The market is Android-heavy or outside the US, where iMessage in particular does not fit

signal.check: RCS or iMessage business messaging is being adopted as a default channel with no holdout test and no check of the list's iPhone share.

expected_effect.size: unknown, expect a fading novelty lift

risk.note: Higher cost per message; verify availability, fees and iPhone share before piloting.

prerequisites: Web check on RCS or iMessage availability, fees and verification
iPhone share of the list
steps: Check RCS or iMessage business messaging availability, fees and verification for the brand's markets.
Check the list's iPhone share before considering iMessage.
Run a holdout test with creative held constant against the standard SMS channel.
Judge the result after accounting for the higher per-message cost, expecting the novelty lift to fade.

test.method: Holdout test comparing the new channel against standard SMS on a matched segment.
test.read_point: After the pilot period, watching for lift decay over time

title: Choose the SMS platform on price and email-platform fit, not AI feature pitches
hypothesis: If the SMS platform is chosen mainly by price and how well it consolidates with the email platform, ignoring AI feature marketing, then cost stays lower and team overhead drops because platform choice matters little to actual results once basic setup is done.

signal.check: A platform decision is being made mainly on an AI feature pitch, with no price comparison against at least 1 other vendor.

risk.note: Vendor selection process; switching costs may apply if changed later.

prerequisites: Quotes from at least 2 SMS vendors
steps: Get a quote from the platform that matches the current email platform.
Get comparison quotes from at least 1 to 2 other vendors.
Decide on price and ease of setup, not AI feature marketing.
Confirm country-specific pricing and registration terms before committing.

test.method: Not a split test; a vendor comparison decision.
test.read_point: Before signing an SMS platform contract

title: Add push notification steps to flows where the brand has an app
hypothesis: If push notification steps are added to flows the same way as SMS, wherever the brand has its own app, then an extra low-cost channel reaches app users who may not check email or SMS as often.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has no branded app

signal.check: The brand has its own app with push capability, but no flow includes a push step.

risk.note: Additive channel; does not replace email or SMS steps.

prerequisites: A branded app with push notification capability
steps: Confirm the app supports push notifications through the email platform or a connected tool.
Add push steps to the same key flows as SMS: welcome, abandonment, post-purchase.
Match push content to the flow's stage, keeping it short.
Track push open and click rate separately from email and SMS.

test.method: Compare recovered revenue with and without the push step for app users.

title: Consider WhatsApp business messaging where SMS is costly and the market is mobile-first
hypothesis: If WhatsApp business messaging is tested in mobile-first, non-US markets where SMS is expensive and iMessage does not fit, then the brand reaches customers on the channel they actually use most, at a lower cost than SMS.
does_not_apply_when: The market is US-based with iMessage fit or SMS is already inexpensive

signal.check: SMS cost per send is high for a mobile-first, non-US market, and WhatsApp business messaging has never been evaluated as an alternative.

risk.note: Web check on WhatsApp business messaging cost and setup in the brand's markets before committing.

prerequisites: Web check on WhatsApp business messaging cost and setup for the brand's markets
steps: Check WhatsApp business messaging cost and setup requirements for the brand's markets.
Compare projected cost per message against current SMS cost.
Pilot with 1 flow, such as order updates or abandonment, before wider rollout.
Track cost per send and engagement against the SMS equivalent.

test.method: Pilot WhatsApp on 1 flow and compare cost and engagement against the SMS version.
test.read_point: After the pilot flow runs for 30 days

title: Decide every test's winning metric as placed order rate or revenue per recipient
hypothesis: If every flow, campaign or subject line test states placed order rate or revenue per recipient as the winning metric before it runs, then test results actually reflect revenue impact because open rate is not a reliable signal once Apple Mail opens every email automatically.

signal.check: A recent test was judged mainly on open rate, or no winning metric was stated before the test ran.

risk.note: Test process discipline, not a live change.

prerequisites: Ability to read placed order rate and revenue per recipient by test variant
steps: Before running any test, write the hypothesis and state placed order rate or revenue per recipient as the winning metric.
Use unique clicks as a secondary signal.
Use open rate, Apple opens excluded, only as a deliverability gate, never as the winning metric.
Judge subject line tests on orders, not opens, unless capacity allows a dedicated subject test.

test.method: Not a split test; a governance rule applied to every future test.
test.measure: Whether a winning metric was stated before each test ran

title: Prioritise tests by revenue impact, flow delay first, CTA colour last
hypothesis: If tests run in priority order, flow delay on the biggest flow first, then content and offer, then long vs short and text vs designed, with CTA colour skipped below a revenue threshold, then testing time pays off faster because effort goes to the changes most likely to move real revenue.
does_not_apply_when: The store is well past the revenue threshold where small design tests, such as CTA colour, start to matter

signal.check: Recent test effort has gone into small design details, such as button colour, while flow delays and offer content have never been tested.

risk.note: Prioritisation only, not a specific test.

prerequisites: List of untested elements across flows and campaigns
steps: List every untested lever: flow delay, content and offer, product vs collection, long vs short, text vs designed, send time, subject lines, CTA colour.
Order the list by expected revenue impact, flow delay in the biggest flow first.
Skip granular tests like CTA colour under about 100,000 dollars a month in revenue.
Work down the list 1 test at a time.

test.method: Not a split test; a prioritisation method applied to the testing roadmap.
test.read_point: After each completed test on the list

title: A/B test plain text against a fully designed version of the same message
hypothesis: If a plain-text version and a fully designed version of the same flow email or campaign are tested against each other, then the brand learns which format actually converts better for its own audience, since sources disagree on which wins by default.

signal.check: The brand has always used 1 format, either fully designed or plain text, with no test comparing the two on the same message.

risk.note: A/B test within an existing flow or campaign slot.

prerequisites: Both a plain-text and a designed version of the same message
steps: Pick a flow email or campaign to test.
Write a plain-text version and build a fully designed version with the same core message.
Run a manual 50/50 split test.
Judge on placed order rate or revenue per recipient, not opens.

test.method: Manual 50/50 A/B test, judged on placed order rate.
test.read_point: After 1,000 recipients per branch for a flow, or 5 to 10 sends for a campaign

title: Duplicate every downstream email onto both branches of a flow timing test
hypothesis: If a flow timing test duplicates every following email onto both branches instead of rejoining them after email 1, then the test result stays clean because merging branches early mixes the 2 timing conditions together and makes the read unreliable.

signal.check: A flow timing test rejoins its 2 branches back into 1 path after the first email.

expected_effect.size: test accuracy improvement, not a revenue-size claim

risk.note: Test structure fix only.

prerequisites: A flow timing test already planned or running
steps: Set up the conditional split for the timing test at the first delay.
Duplicate every remaining email in the flow onto both the A and B branches.
Do not rejoin the branches after email 1.
Read results per branch through to the end of the flow.

test.method: Not a separate test; a structural rule applied to every flow timing test.
test.measure: Whether both branches stay fully separate through the flow
test.read_point: Before launching any flow timing test

title: Set clean attribution: exclude transactional, bot clicks and Apple opens
hypothesis: If attribution excludes transactional messages, bot clicks and Apple privacy opens, with about a 5-day window for email and 1 day for SMS, then reported email revenue becomes trustworthy because inflated attribution otherwise hides whether the program is actually working.

signal.check: Attribution settings still use platform defaults, with transactional messages, bot clicks or Apple opens included.

expected_effect.size: reported revenue is expected to fall once inflated attribution is removed

risk.note: Reporting change; note prior values before changing for a clean before-and-after comparison.

prerequisites: Web check on the platform's current attribution defaults
steps: Note current reported revenue before changing anything, for a before-and-after comparison.
Set the attribution window to about 5 days, open and click, last interacted.
Exclude Apple Mail Privacy Protection opens.
Exclude transactional messages and bot clicks for both email and SMS.
Set the SMS attribution window to about 1 day.
Shorten the window for impulse products, lengthen it for long-consideration purchases.

test.method: Not a split test; compare reported revenue before and after the settings change.
test.read_point: Immediately after the change, and again after 30 days

title: Turn on anonymous visitor tracking so pre-signup activity feeds flows
hypothesis: If anonymous visitor tracking is turned on, then browse and cart flows work correctly for people who browsed before signing up, because their pre-signup views and carts backfill onto their profile once they subscribe.

signal.check: Anonymous visitor tracking is off, so browse or cart flows sometimes miss activity that happened before a person subscribed.

risk.note: Setting toggle only.

prerequisites: Platform support for anonymous visitor tracking
steps: Turn on anonymous visitor tracking in the account settings.
Confirm UTM parameters are set to automatically add to links.
Test by browsing anonymously, then signing up, and checking that the prior activity appears on the profile.
Confirm browse and cart flows correctly pick up the backfilled activity.

test.method: Not a split test; a functional check with a real test signup.
test.measure: Whether pre-signup activity backfills onto the new profile

title: Read the full metric chain before diagnosing a campaign or flow problem
hypothesis: If a drop in revenue is diagnosed by walking the full chain from recipients through opens, clicks, conversions and revenue instead of reading the headline number alone, then the actual cause gets fixed because opens down points to deliverability while clicks down with steady opens points to content.

signal.check: A revenue drop is discussed only at the headline level, with no read through opens, clicks and conversion rate to find where the drop actually starts.

expected_effect.size: diagnostic accuracy, not a direct revenue claim

risk.note: Diagnostic method, not a live change.

prerequisites: Reporting broken out by recipients, opens, clicks, conversions, revenue
steps: Pull recipients, unique opens, open rate, unique clicks, click rate, unique conversions, conversion rate, revenue and revenue per recipient.
Find the first stage in the chain where the number moved more than about 10 percent.
If opens dropped, suspect deliverability. If clicks dropped with opens steady, suspect content. If conversions dropped with clicks steady, suspect merchandising or offer.
Read revenue and order count together to catch an AOV-driven distortion.
Treat under 5 percent moves as noise.

test.method: Not a split test; a diagnostic method applied whenever a metric moves.
test.measure: The full metric chain by campaign or flow
test.read_point: Whenever a metric moves more than about 10 percent

title: Check site traffic before flagging a flow revenue drop as a flow problem
hypothesis: If a flow revenue drop is checked against site traffic first, then time is not wasted fixing a healthy flow, because flow revenue follows site traffic and a drop is only a real flag if traffic held steady.

signal.check: A flow revenue drop is being investigated with no comparison to site traffic over the same period.

expected_effect.size: diagnostic accuracy, not a direct revenue claim

risk.note: Diagnostic method, not a live change.

prerequisites: Site traffic data alongside flow revenue
steps: Pull site traffic for the same period as the flow revenue drop.
If traffic also dropped, the flow revenue drop likely follows traffic, not a flow problem.
If traffic held steady, check the flow itself for skips, filters and dynamic block issues.
Only rebuild flow content once traffic has been ruled out as the cause.

test.method: Not a split test; a diagnostic method applied whenever flow revenue drops.
test.measure: flow_revenue_share against sessions over the same period

title: Run a mandatory monthly review to catch silent breakage
hypothesis: If a monthly review checks list growth, popup views, flow sends, campaign mix and deliverability against the prior month, then silent breakage, a theme update hiding the popup, a stalled flow, a broken integration, gets caught early because none of these throw a visible error on their own.

signal.check: No monthly review has run in the last 30 to 45 days, or the last review found no issues despite known volatility in the store's theme, apps or integrations.

risk.note: Review process, not a live change by itself.

prerequisites: Access to list growth, popup, flow, campaign and deliverability reporting
steps: Check list growth: gains vs losses, opt-in sources vs prior month.
Check each popup's views and submit rate vs the prior 30 days.
Check campaigns by revenue, clicks, placed orders, and note the lowest performers.
Check flow revenue vs site traffic, then the metric chain, then top flows vs last month.
Check the deliverability tab against the section 6 thresholds.
Run the monthly suppression.
Check SMS cadence, clicks, unsubscribes, delivery and net profit.
Write the month's 3 findings and the next 3 tests into the tracker.

test.method: Not a split test; a recurring monthly process.
test.measure: Number of issues caught per monthly review

title: Never send a fake restock, sell-out or scarcity message
hypothesis: If every restock, sell-out or running-low message reflects a real inventory event, then customer trust holds because a customer who discovers a fake scarcity claim discounts every future urgency message from the brand.

signal.check: A restock, sell-out or running-low message has been sent that did not match a real inventory event.

risk.note: Content honesty check.

prerequisites: Real-time inventory data
steps: Check every restock or scarcity message against real inventory data before sending.
Remove any stated deadline or stock level that is not accurate.
Apply the same check to any resetting countdown timer.
Add this to the pre-send checklist for any urgency-based copy.

test.method: Not a split test; a compliance and trust check before every urgency-based send.
test.measure: Whether every scarcity claim matches real inventory data
test.read_point: Before every send using scarcity or restock messaging

title: Never use invisible text tricks to pad an email
hypothesis: If no email uses invisible or near-invisible text, such as tiny background-coloured content, then deliverability holds because this is a known spam signal that inbox providers actively look for.

signal.check: An email template includes text sized or coloured to be effectively invisible to the reader.

risk.note: Template fix only.

prerequisites: Access to inspect the email's underlying code
steps: Inspect the email source for any tiny or background-colour-matched text.
Remove any invisible text found.
Replace with visible live text using the live-text approach where extra content is needed.
Recheck any inherited template for this pattern.

test.method: Not a split test; a template inspection check.
test.measure: Whether any invisible text is present in the template
test.read_point: Before adopting or reusing any template

title: Keep a visible close on every popup step, never hidden
hypothesis: If every popup step keeps a visible X plus a clear no thanks button, then trust and accessibility hold because a hidden or near-invisible close forces a decision through deception rather than a genuine yes.

signal.check: Any popup step has an X sized, coloured or positioned to be hard to see, or the success step has no way to close it.

risk.note: Design fix only.

prerequisites: Access to the popup builder
steps: Check every popup step, including the success step, for a visible close.
Restore a clearly visible X and a no thanks button wherever missing or hidden.
Owners may test a smaller or repositioned X, but never a hidden one.
Check accessibility and interstitial guidance where relevant.

test.method: Not a split test; a design and trust check.
test.measure: Whether every popup step has a visible close

title: Check consent, quiet-hours and sender-registration rules live before any new market's SMS send
hypothesis: If consent wording, quiet hours and sender registration are checked live for the recipient's actual country before every new market's first SMS send, then the brand avoids applying US-only assumptions to a market with different rules, such as India's DLT registration requirement.

signal.check: SMS is expanding into a new country with no country-specific check on consent wording, quiet hours or sender registration.

risk.note: Sending SMS in a new market without checking local rules risks fines or blocked sends.

prerequisites: Web check on consent, quiet hours and sender registration per country
steps: Before any first send in a new market, check consent wording requirements for that country.
Check the legal quiet-hours window for that country and any relevant state or region.
Check sender registration requirements, such as toll-free, short code, or India's DLT header and template approval.
Sign off on a compliance checklist before the first send in that market.

test.method: Not a split test; a compliance sign-off before every new market's SMS launch.
test.measure: Whether the compliance checklist is signed off before the first send
test.read_point: Before every new market's SMS launch

title: Never fake a person or an automated message from a human
hypothesis: If the brand always identifies itself as the sender and never uses deliberate typos or a fake persona to make an automated message look human, then long-term trust holds because customers who discover the trick discount every future message from the brand.

signal.check: A message uses deliberate typos, presents an automated send as a spontaneous personal text, or otherwise disguises the brand as sender.

risk.note: Copy and process check only.

prerequisites: Copy review process before send
steps: Review any conversational SMS or founder-voice email copy for fake typos or an implied fake persona.
Confirm the store is clearly identified as the sender in every message.
Remove any tactic designed to disguise an automated send as a spontaneous human one.
Keep this as a standing rule in the copy review checklist.

test.method: Not a split test; a copy review check before every send.
test.measure: Whether the sender is honestly identified in every message

title: Use competitor emails and ads for layout and mood only, never copy them
hypothesis: If competitor emails and ads are used only for layout and mood signals, with AI-assisted structure analysis allowed but no verbatim reuse of their text, logos, products or faces, then the brand avoids a copyright or trademark issue while still learning from what is working in the category.

signal.check: A draft closely copies a competitor's exact wording, logo, product shot or a person's face from their marketing.

risk.note: Verbatim reuse of a competitor's assets is a legal risk.

prerequisites: Competitor emails or ads gathered for research
steps: Use competitor emails and ads only to note layout, mood and general structure.
Allow AI-assisted structural analysis, such as summarising the flow of a competitor's page.
Never copy their exact text, logo, product images or a person's face.
Check every draft against this boundary before it ships.

test.method: Not a split test; a content review check.
test.measure: Whether any draft too closely matches a competitor's exact assets
test.read_point: Before every send that drew on competitor research

title: Compute lifecycle metrics in code from exports, never estimate them
hypothesis: If revenue per recipient, opt-in rate, net profit per SMS and segment counts are always computed in code from real exports, with missing values shown as unavailable rather than zero, then reported numbers stay trustworthy because a human-estimated or eyeballed figure is far more likely to be wrong.

signal.check: A reported number, such as revenue per recipient or opt-in rate, was estimated or eyeballed instead of computed from an export.

expected_effect.size: reporting accuracy, not a direct revenue claim

risk.note: Process discipline only.

prerequisites: Export access to the platform's raw data
steps: Pull the raw export for the metric in question rather than reading a rounded dashboard number alone.
Compute the metric in code or a spreadsheet formula, not by eye.
Show any missing or unsupported value as unavailable, never as zero.
Apply this rule to every reported number in the monthly review.

test.method: Not a split test; a reporting-accuracy rule applied to every report.
test.measure: Whether every reported metric traces back to a real export computation

title: Run the full tracking and account setup checklist before building any flow
hypothesis: If Shopify sync, sender identity, attribution, UTM, brand library and consent pages are all confirmed set up before any flow build starts, then every flow built afterward reports cleanly and looks on-brand from day 1, instead of needing rework later.

signal.check: Flows are being built on a new account with no confirmed Shopify sync, sender identity, attribution settings, UTM, brand library or consent pages.

risk.note: Setup checklist; each item is individually reversible.

prerequisites: Admin access to the email platform and the storefront
steps: Confirm the Shopify or storefront integration syncs email and SMS subscribers into the right lists.
Set sender name, sender email on the brand domain, and reply-to at support.
Set Smart Sending, attribution window and exclusions per the attribution idea.
Turn on anonymous visitor tracking and UTM parameters.
Load the brand library: logo, colours, fonts with fallbacks, social links.
Brand the consent, unsubscribe and confirmation pages.
Send a test campaign to 1 profile and confirm UTM and open and click tracking work.

test.method: Not a split test; a one-time setup checklist run before flow building begins.
test.measure: Whether every checklist item passes its test send
test.read_point: Before building the first flow on a new or newly audited account

title: Authenticate the sending domain and ramp DMARC from none to reject
hypothesis: If a branded sending domain is fully authenticated and DMARC starts at none with reporting, then moves to quarantine and eventually reject once every legitimate source aligns, then deliverability improves over time because the domain builds a clean, provable sending identity instead of relying on a shared or unauthenticated one.

signal.check: The account sends from a shared or unauthenticated domain, or has no DMARC record, or DMARC has sat at none with no plan to move up.

risk.note: Moving DMARC to quarantine or reject too early can block legitimate mail; read reports first.

prerequisites: Access to the domain's DNS records
steps: Add the root domain and choose a sending subdomain in the email platform.
Add every DNS record the platform lists.
Wait for verification, up to 48 hours, before sending from the new domain.
Add a DMARC TXT record starting at p=none with a reporting address.
Read DMARC reports for 2 to 4 weeks.
Move to p=quarantine once every legitimate source aligns, then to p=reject.
Limit sends to the engaged segment for 2 to 4 weeks after the domain goes live, as a warm-up.

test.method: Run a DMARC checker and a placement test after each policy step-up.
test.read_point: After each 2 to 4 week reporting period before stepping up the policy

title: Test a predictive smart-trigger popup against fixed delay rules
hypothesis: If a popup platform's predictive smart-trigger option, which fires once based on a visitor behaviour model instead of a fixed delay or scroll percent, is tested against the current fixed rule, then signup rate or total signups may rise because the model can time the offer to each visitor's own browsing pattern instead of 1 rule for everyone.
does_not_apply_when: The popup platform has no predictive or smart-trigger timing feature

signal.check: The popup only uses a fixed time delay or scroll percent trigger, and the platform offers an unused predictive or smart-trigger timing option.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one vendor reports signup rate slightly lower but total signups higher in some accounts, reversed in others

risk.note: Only changes when the popup fires; easy to revert to the fixed rule.

prerequisites: A popup platform with a predictive or smart-trigger timing feature
steps: Note current signup rate and total signups under the fixed delay or scroll trigger.
Turn on the predictive smart-trigger option as an A/B test variant against the fixed rule.
Run until each side has enough impressions per the account's own test-size rule.
Compare signup rate and total signups together, not signup rate alone.
Keep whichever version wins on total signups and downstream welcome flow revenue.

test.method: A/B test: fixed delay or scroll trigger vs predictive smart trigger, 50/50 split.
test.read_point: After the platform's minimum test size is reached

title: Use popup quiz answers to find and target the best-converting segment
hypothesis: If a 1-question popup quiz's answers are stored as zero-party data and reviewed for purchase rate by answer, then the store can send extra targeted content to the highest-converting answer group because the quiz reveals intent the store did not have to guess at.

signal.check: A popup quiz or micro-commit question collects an answer that is stored on the profile but never reviewed for purchase rate by answer, and no follow-up content is built from it.

risk.note: Reporting and targeting change; no live disruption to the popup itself.

prerequisites: A popup quiz step that writes its answer to the subscriber profile
Enough order history to compute purchase rate by answer
steps: Confirm the quiz answer is saved as a profile property or tag.
Pull purchase rate and revenue per subscriber for each answer group.
Identify the answer group with the strongest purchase rate.
Build 1 to 2 extra emails or a short flow aimed only at that group.
Track whether the targeted group's conversion improves against its own baseline.

test.method: Not a split test; a segmentation and targeting analysis repeated each quarter.
test.read_point: After enough orders accumulate per answer group, then quarterly

title: Run a seed-list inbox placement test alongside open rate
hypothesis: If a monthly seed-list placement test and a per-inbox-provider and per-country breakdown are read alongside open rate, then deliverability problems get caught earlier because open rate alone cannot show whether mail is landing in the inbox, promotions or spam, or which provider is actually the weak point.

signal.check: Deliverability is judged only from the account's own open rate trend, with no seed-list placement test and no read of performance broken out by inbox provider or country.

risk.note: Diagnostic only; some placement-test tools charge a small monthly fee.

prerequisites: A seed-list placement testing tool
Access to the platform's deliverability tab by inbox provider and country
steps: Send a routine test campaign through a seed-list placement tool once a month.
Read the inbox vs promotions vs spam split, plus any blocklist or IP reputation flag.
Open the platform's deliverability report broken out by inbox provider and by country.
Flag any single provider or country far below the account average.
Build a tighter engaged segment for that provider or country before sending there again.

test.method: Not a split test; a recurring monthly diagnostic.
test.measure: Inbox placement share, plus opens and clicks by provider and country

title: Send 1 to 3 plain-text-only campaigns a month as ongoing practice
hypothesis: If 1 to 3 campaigns a month go out as plain text with no image blocks, on an ongoing basis rather than as a one-off test, then the account stays readable to AI-driven inbox filters because the content makes sense even when images and a designed layout are stripped away.

signal.check: Every campaign in the last month used a fully designed, image-heavy layout, with no plain-text sends on a recurring schedule.

risk.note: A content-mix change, easy to adjust the ratio.

prerequisites: A monthly campaign calendar to schedule the plain-text slots into
steps: Pick 1 to 3 send slots a month to run as plain text with no images.
Write the same core message as a designed send would carry, in short paragraphs.
Keep the sender identity and reply-to the same as every other send.
Send to the normal engaged segment, not a special list.
Track opens, clicks and placement alongside designed sends over the following months.

test.method: Not a controlled test; an ongoing content-mix practice compared to prior months.
test.measure: other:spam_rate and click rate trend after adding plain-text sends
test.read_point: After 2 to 3 months of the new mix

title: Suppress never-emailed and no-activity-in-a-year profiles
hypothesis: If profiles that were never emailed, or that have shown no email or site activity in over a year since first joining, are suppressed as their own segment rather than folded into the recent-activity unengaged rule, then list cost and spam risk drop because these dead-on-arrival profiles never had a chance to become engaged and are not caught by a rolling recent-activity window.

signal.check: List cleaning only checks recent open and click windows, with no separate check for profiles that were added a year or more ago and have never opened, clicked or visited the site since.

risk.note: Suppression can be reversed for any profile if needed.

prerequisites: A platform that tracks first-active or created date on profiles
steps: Build a segment: first active or created at least 1 year ago AND received email 0 times over all time.
Build a second segment: first active or created at least 1 year ago AND received email 0 times AND no site activity in the last year.
Review both segments' size.
Suppress both segments alongside the normal monthly unengaged suppression.
Repeat the check monthly as new profiles age past 1 year.

test.method: Not a split test; a recurring list-hygiene action.

title: Invite replies in email campaigns to build a deliverability signal
hypothesis: If some campaigns end with a genuine question and an invitation to reply, such as ask us anything, and the reply inbox is staffed, then inbox placement improves because a reply is one of the strongest engagement signals AI-driven inboxes read, and it is a signal marketing email rarely earns.

signal.check: No recent campaign has invited a reply, and the sending address either cannot receive replies or nobody is watching it.

risk.note: Requires someone to monitor and answer the reply inbox.

prerequisites: A sending address that accepts replies
Someone assigned to read and answer replies
steps: Confirm the sender address accepts replies and someone checks it daily.
Pick 1 upcoming campaign to end with a direct, real question inviting a reply.
Send to the normal engaged segment.
Log reply volume and answer every reply within a stated window.
Repeat on a recurring basis and watch inbox placement and click rate over following sends.

test.method: Not a split test; an ongoing engagement practice tracked against placement over time.
test.measure: Reply count and inbox placement rate before and after adding reply-inviting sends
test.read_point: After 2 to 3 months of regular reply-inviting sends

title: Test first-person CTA copy against second-person CTA copy
hypothesis: If a popup or email CTA is tested in first person, such as claim my discount, against the same CTA in second person, such as claim your discount, then signup or click rate may rise because a first-person CTA can make the action feel like the reader's own choice rather than an instruction.

signal.check: Every CTA on the popup and in emails uses second-person wording, and first-person CTA copy has never been tested.

risk.note: Copy-only change, reversible instantly.

prerequisites: An A/B testable popup or email CTA button
steps: Pick 1 CTA to test, on the popup or in a high-volume flow email.
Write a first-person version, such as claim my discount, keeping every other element the same.
Run a 50/50 test against the current second-person CTA.
Judge on signup rate or placed order rate, not clicks alone.
Roll out the winner and note the result for future CTA copy.

test.method: A/B test, first-person vs second-person CTA copy, 50/50 split.
test.measure: signup rate or placed order rate
test.read_point: After the account's normal test-size rule is met

title: Test popup image hierarchy: pets, faces, then product-only shots
hypothesis: If a popup or hero image is tested across a pet image, a human face looking toward the headline, and a plain product shot, then signup or click rate differences show which image type actually earns attention for this brand, because reported image hierarchies do not generalise across brands.

signal.check: The popup or hero image type has never been split tested, and the current choice was picked by preference rather than a result.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one reported example moved from a no-image control to a large lift with a pet image, but the source warns not to generalise

risk.note: Image-only change, reversible instantly.

prerequisites: Usable images for at least 2 of the 3 image types
steps: Prepare a pet image, a human-face image looking toward the headline, and a plain product image, sized the same.
Run each as a popup or hero variant against the others, or against the current no-image control.
Hold the offer and copy constant across variants.
Judge on signup rate or click rate, not visual preference.
Keep the winner and re-test if the brand's imagery library changes.

test.method: A/B or multi-variant test across image types, 1 variable changed.
test.read_point: After the account's normal test-size rule is met

title: Track click, spam complaint and unsubscribe rate, not open rate alone
hypothesis: If every campaign is checked against click rate, spam complaint rate and unsubscribe rate targets, not only an open rate target, then declining sender health is caught earlier because open rate is inflated by Apple Mail privacy protection and can look healthy while clicks, complaints or unsubscribes are already moving the wrong way.

signal.check: Campaign health is reviewed on open rate alone, with no stated target or tracked trend for click rate, spam complaint rate or unsubscribe rate.

risk.note: Reporting change only.

prerequisites: Campaign-level reporting on click, spam complaint and unsubscribe rate
steps: Pull click rate, spam complaint rate and unsubscribe rate for the last 10 to 20 campaigns.
Set a working floor for each, informed by platform guidance and the brand's own history.
Add all 3 to the standard post-send or monthly review, alongside open rate.
Flag any campaign or trend that crosses a floor even if open rate looks fine.
Investigate content, audience or technical causes before the next send.

test.method: Not a split test; a recurring reporting and review practice.
test.measure: click rate, spam complaint rate and unsubscribe rate trend

title: Vary the popup discount by traffic source or cart value
hypothesis: If the popup shows a smaller discount to cheap or already-converting paid traffic and a special offer only above a cart value threshold, using UTM source or cart value rules, then margin improves because the same flat discount is no longer given to visitors who would have converted for less or who are already deep in the funnel.
does_not_apply_when: The popup platform cannot target by UTM source or cart value

signal.check: Every visitor sees the same popup offer regardless of traffic source or current cart value, on a platform that supports UTM or cart-value targeting rules.

risk.note: Different offers by visitor can look inconsistent if visitors compare notes; keep the logic simple and defensible.

prerequisites: Popup targeting rules by UTM parameter or cart value
Margin data by offer size
steps: Identify 1 or 2 traffic sources with the cheapest cost per click or highest existing conversion rate.
Set a smaller popup discount for those UTM sources, and the standard discount for everyone else.
Optionally add a cart-value rule offering a different incentive only above a set cart total.
Track signup rate, welcome flow conversion and margin per rule versus the flat-offer baseline.
Adjust or remove the rule if signup rate drops more than the margin gain justifies.

test.method: Before-and-after comparison of margin and signup rate by traffic source after adding the rule.
test.measure: discount_rate and gross_margin by traffic source
test.read_point: After 30 to 60 days of the rule running

title: Test sending abandonment email and SMS at nearly the same time
hypothesis: If an abandonment flow sends email and SMS within minutes of each other instead of staggering SMS after a wait for email to fail, then recovered revenue may rise because the store cannot know in advance which channel a given shopper will act on first, and staggering delays the channel that would have converted.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has an SMS program
SMS consent is not yet collected

signal.check: The abandonment flow always waits a fixed period after email before sending SMS, or vice versa, with no test of sending both close together.

risk.note: Timing-only change within an existing flow.

prerequisites: Both email and SMS steps already built into the same abandonment flow
steps: Note current recovered revenue under the staggered email-then-SMS pattern.
Change the SMS delay to fire within a few minutes of the email instead of after a wait.
Keep both messages' content and offer identical to the staggered version.
Run for enough abandoners to compare recovered revenue and unsubscribe or opt-out rate.
Keep whichever pattern converts more without raising opt-outs.

test.method: Flow-level A/B test: staggered vs near-simultaneous email and SMS send.
test.read_point: After enough abandoners pass through both branches

title: Flag sunset-flow completers with a persistent profile property
hypothesis: If the sunset flow writes a permanent unengaged property to a profile once someone completes it without engaging, and suppression runs off that property instead of a rolling activity window, then suppression stays stable and auditable because the flag does not change back and forth as the recent-activity window rolls forward.

signal.check: Suppression is computed only from a rolling opened or clicked window, so a profile can drop in and out of the unengaged segment as the window moves, with no permanent record of having completed the sunset flow.

risk.note: The property can be cleared manually if a profile re-engages later.

prerequisites: A sunset flow with a final no-engagement branch
The platform supports writable profile properties
steps: Add a boolean profile property, such as unengaged, defaulted to false.
At the end of the sunset flow, set the property to true for anyone who never opened or clicked during it.
Build the suppression segment on that property being true, alongside the can-receive-marketing condition.
Suppress that segment monthly, independent of the rolling engaged window.
Clear the property manually if a suppressed profile later opens or orders.

test.method: Not a split test; a suppression-mechanism change tracked for stability over following months.

title: Choose static or dynamic product blocks by catalogue turnover
hypothesis: If a brand with fast-turning inventory and frequent new styles uses a dynamic, rule-based product feed while a brand with a small, stable catalogue uses a static, hand-picked product block, then campaign and flow content stays relevant with less manual upkeep because the mechanism matches how often the catalogue actually changes.

signal.check: Every email uses the same block type, either always static or always dynamic, regardless of how often the catalogue's bestsellers or in-stock items actually change.

risk.note: Block-type change only.

prerequisites: Email platform support for both static and dynamic, rule-based product blocks
steps: Assess catalogue size and how often bestsellers or in-stock status change.
For a fast-turning or large catalogue, build a dynamic feed with rules such as bestselling in the last 90 days, excluding low stock.
For a small, stable catalogue, hand-pick 2 to 3 steady bestsellers as a static block.
Update the static block manually on a fixed schedule if items change.
Recheck the choice if the catalogue's turnover changes materially.

test.method: Not a split test; a fit-to-catalogue decision, reviewed if the catalogue changes.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart and manual maintenance time on the block
test.read_point: When the catalogue's size or turnover changes

title: Use show/hide logic to personalise 1 email for several audiences
hypothesis: If a single email uses show/hide logic on a profile property, such as country, unused-offer status or loyalty points balance, then 1 build serves several audiences correctly because the content adapts per recipient instead of requiring a separate email for each version.

signal.check: The account builds separate near-duplicate emails for each audience variant, such as by country or loyalty status, when the platform supports show/hide logic on 1 email instead.

risk.note: Test each condition with a real profile per branch before sending; a wrong condition can show the wrong content to the wrong group.

prerequisites: Email platform support for show/hide logic on profile properties
steps: Pick 1 recurring email that currently exists in several near-duplicate versions, such as by country or loyalty status.
Add a text or content block with show/hide logic keyed to the relevant profile property.
Duplicate the block for each condition and its opposite or alternative value.
Preview and test with a real profile representing each condition before sending.
Retire the separate duplicate emails once the single dynamic version is confirmed correct.

test.method: Not a split test; a build-mechanism change verified by preview across profile conditions.
test.measure: Correctness across preview profiles, and build time per send
test.read_point: Before the first live send, then ongoing

title: Push high-engagement email segments to ad platforms for lookalikes
hypothesis: If a high-engagement or high-LTV email segment is pushed to Meta or Google through an integration for retargeting and lookalike audiences, then paid acquisition efficiency improves because the ad platform can find more people who resemble the store's own best customers instead of relying only on its own conversion data.
does_not_apply_when: The email platform has no ads integration
The segment is too small for the ad platform's minimum audience size

signal.check: High-value or highly engaged email segments exist but are never pushed to any ad platform for retargeting or lookalike audience building.

risk.note: Turning off the sync stops future pushes; it does not undo audiences already built by the ad platform.

prerequisites: An ads integration connected to the email or CRM platform
A defined high-engagement or high-LTV segment
steps: Pick 1 segment, such as VIPs or high predicted lifetime value, with enough profiles to meet the ad platform's minimum.
Connect the ads integration and push that segment as a custom audience.
Build a lookalike or similar audience from it in the ad platform.
Run it as a distinct campaign or ad set so its performance can be read on its own.
Compare its cost per acquisition and return against the account's other prospecting audiences.

test.method: Compare the lookalike audience's performance against the account's standard prospecting audience.
test.measure: ncpa and roas_prospecting for the lookalike audience
test.read_point: After the lookalike audience has enough spend to read a result

title: Build a win-the-pause-back flow off the subscription pause event
hypothesis: If a subscription pause event triggers its own short recovery flow, separate from the charge-reminder and failed-payment flows, then paused subscribers resume sooner because a paused customer gets a direct, timed nudge to unpause instead of only hearing from the brand again at the next skipped charge attempt.
does_not_apply_when: The subscription app does not expose a pause event to the email or SMS platform

signal.check: Subscribers who pause get no dedicated message until the next charge attempt or a generic winback flow, with no flow triggered directly on the pause event.

risk.note: New flow addition; does not change the pause mechanic itself.

prerequisites: A subscription app that exposes a pause event to the email platform
steps: Confirm the subscription app's pause event is available as a flow trigger.
Build a flow triggered on that event, exiting anyone who resumes or cancels.
Send a first email soon after the pause confirming the pause and offering a 1-click resume link.
Send a second message partway through the paused period asking what would bring them back.
Send a final message shortly before the pause would otherwise lapse into cancellation.

test.method: Compare resume rate for paused subscribers with the flow live against the prior resume rate without it.
test.measure: subscription_churn and resume rate among paused subscribers

title: Build a tighter engaged segment for an underperforming inbox provider
hypothesis: If deliverability data shows 1 inbox provider, such as Hotmail or Outlook, with materially lower opens and clicks or higher bounce than the account average, then building a tighter, more-engaged-only segment for that provider and sending there separately helps recover its reputation because a provider-wide problem needs a provider-specific fix, not a blanket account-wide change.

signal.check: Deliverability reporting by inbox provider shows 1 provider well below the account average on opens or clicks, or well above on bounce or spam complaints, with no separate segment or sending plan for that provider.

risk.note: Segment-level sending change, reversible at any time.

prerequisites: Deliverability reporting broken out by inbox provider
steps: Read the deliverability report by inbox provider and identify any clear underperformer.
Build an engaged segment scoped to that provider's domains with a shorter engagement window than the account default.
Send that provider's recipients only to this tighter segment for several sends.
Track that provider's open, click and bounce rate against the rest of the account.
Widen the window again once the provider's metrics recover toward the account average.

test.method: Before-and-after comparison of the provider's metrics after switching to the tighter segment.
test.measure: Open, click and bounce rate for the affected provider
test.read_point: After several sends to the tighter provider-specific segment

title: Send a pure-engagement newsletter with no selling
hypothesis: If a regular newsletter carries no product pitch at all, curated or created content such as industry news, a playlist, or light brand-relevant humour, then open and click habits strengthen because a send built purely to be worth opening earns attention that pure product content cannot, and that habit carries over to product-focused sends.

signal.check: Every regular campaign includes a product pitch or CTA to buy, with no recurring send built purely for engagement.

risk.note: Content-mix change; does not touch flows or existing promo cadence.

prerequisites: A recurring campaign slot to dedicate to this format
steps: Pick a recurring slot, such as monthly or every other week, for a no-selling newsletter.
Curate or create content the audience would want regardless of purchase intent, matched to brand voice.
Include at most 1 soft, optional link, never a hard CTA to buy.
Send to the normal engaged segment and track opens and clicks against product-focused sends.
Keep the format only if it holds or lifts engagement over several sends.

test.method: Compare open and click rate of the newsletter format against the account's product-focused campaigns.
test.measure: email_click_rate for newsletter sends vs product sends

title: Use a persistent in-flow flag to exclude campaigns for the whole flow
hypothesis: If a boolean profile property is set true when someone enters a long flow such as welcome and set false on exit, and every campaign excludes anyone with that property true, then unsubscribes and complaints drop compared to a rolling 24-hour exclusion window, because a multi-day flow can otherwise overlap a campaign well beyond 1 day.

signal.check: Campaign exclusions only cover a short rolling window, such as the last 24 hours, while flows such as welcome or cart and checkout run over several days to 2 weeks, leaving overlap for most of the flow's length.

risk.note: Requires care that the flag is reliably cleared on flow exit, or people stay wrongly excluded.

prerequisites: Platform support for writable profile properties inside a flow
steps: Add a boolean profile property, such as in welcome flow, per flow that needs this.
Set the property true at flow entry and false at flow exit or completion.
Add a campaign exclusion for anyone with any of these properties true.
Tick the setting that determines recipients at send time so the exclusion reflects live status.
Audit periodically that the property clears correctly on every exit path.

test.method: Compare unsubscribe and complaint rate for campaigns before and after the flag-based exclusion replaces the rolling window.
test.read_point: After several campaign sends with the flag-based exclusion live

title: Judge popup or capture changes by full-site conversion, not opt-in alone
hypothesis: If a popup or on-site capture change is tested against full-site conversion rate, not opt-in rate alone, then the store avoids shipping a change that raises signups while quietly hurting checkout, because a popup change can look great on its own metric and still tank overall site conversion.

signal.check: Popup or capture tests are judged only on signup or opt-in rate, with no check of full-site conversion rate before and after the change ships.

expected_effect.size: unknown, this is a guardrail against a hidden drop, not a claimed lift

risk.note: Adds a check; does not change the popup itself.

prerequisites: Site-wide conversion rate tracking separate from popup analytics
steps: Record full-site conversion rate for the period before any popup or capture change ships.
Ship the popup or capture change as usual, tracked as a full-site experiment where possible.
Record signup rate and full-site conversion rate for a matched period after the change.
If signup rate rose but full-site conversion fell, treat the change as a loss and revert or redesign it.
Only keep changes that hold or improve full-site conversion alongside signup rate.

test.method: Before-and-after, ideally a holdout, comparing full-site conversion rate around a popup or capture change.
test.read_point: After the change has run long enough to read a stable conversion rate

title: Add an RCS add-to-calendar action to launch and drop announcements
hypothesis: If an RCS message sent about a week before a launch or drop includes a native add-to-calendar action button instead of a plain watch this space line, then more subscribers show up on launch day because the reminder is set on their phone without them having to remember or take a second step.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has no RCS-enabled sending platform
The market has no RCS availability

signal.check: Launch or drop announcements go out as plain SMS or RCS text with no calendar action, and the platform supports an RCS calendar action button.

risk.note: RCS falls back to plain SMS on phones that cannot receive it.

prerequisites: An RCS-capable messaging platform with SMS fallback
A confirmed launch or drop date
steps: Confirm the platform supports an RCS add-to-calendar action and SMS fallback for phones that cannot receive RCS.
About a week before the launch, send an RCS message naming the date and offering an add-to-calendar button.
Fall back to a plain date-and-reminder line for SMS-only recipients.
Track how many recipients added the event versus just received the message, if the platform reports it.
Compare launch-day conversion for this send against a prior launch that used no calendar action.

test.method: Before-and-after comparison of launch-day conversion with and without the calendar action.

title: Answer conversational product questions with an RCS recommendation carousel
hypothesis: If a shopper's conversational question, such as asking what to buy for a certain person or use case, is answered with a native RCS carousel of a few recommended products opening a web view in the thread, instead of bare text links, then conversion rises because the shopper can browse and decide inside the same conversation instead of leaving it.
does_not_apply_when: The brand runs no conversational SMS or RCS program
The messaging platform has no carousel format

signal.check: Conversational replies to product-recommendation questions send plain text links, on a platform that supports an RCS carousel format.

expected_effect.size: unknown, described by the source as a planned direction, not a proven result

risk.note: Falls back to plain text links on non-RCS phones.

prerequisites: A conversational SMS or RCS program with staffed or AI-assisted replies
RCS carousel support on the messaging platform
steps: Identify recurring conversational questions that ask for a recommendation.
Build a short carousel of 3 relevant products with images and prices for the most common request types.
Reply to a matching question with the carousel instead of plain links, opening a web view in-thread.
Fall back to plain text links for recipients whose phone cannot receive RCS.
Track conversion and average order value for carousel replies against plain-link replies.

test.method: Compare conversion and AOV for carousel replies versus plain-text-link replies to similar questions.
test.measure: cvr_overall and aov by reply format
test.read_point: After enough conversational replies of each type to compare

title: Turn conversation reply themes into static and ephemeral customer facts
hypothesis: If replies from conversational SMS or email are tagged as either static facts, such as a product bought or a stated use case, or ephemeral facts that change over time, such as a child's age or a seasonal location, and both are pushed to the CRM, then new flows can trigger on the ephemeral facts because the store now has real customer knowledge instead of only device and click data.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has no conversational reply volume worth mining
There is no CRM or CDP to receive the attributes

signal.check: Conversational replies are read once and then discarded, with no distinction between facts that stay true and facts that will change, and no attribute pushed to the CRM to drive future messages.

risk.note: Storing personal or health-adjacent details from replies raises data protection questions; check local rules before storing sensitive facts.

prerequisites: A way to query or tag conversational replies
A CRM or CDP field structure that can hold custom attributes
steps: Read a sample of recent conversational replies and note recurring fact types.
Classify each fact type as static, does not change, or ephemeral, expected to change over time.
Push static facts to the CRM as stable profile properties.
Push ephemeral facts with a review or refresh date attached, so stale facts get re-asked or expired.
Build 1 new flow or personalised message off an ephemeral fact, such as a seasonal or life-stage change.

test.method: Not a split test; a data-capture and flow-building process, evaluated by whether it produces a usable new trigger.
test.measure: other:ltv_from_conversation for customers with captured attributes versus without
test.read_point: After enough conversation volume to populate attributes and build at least 1 flow

title: Review or suppress long-tenure SMS subscribers who never bought
hypothesis: If SMS subscribers who joined a year or more ago and have never placed an order are reviewed and either sent a direct objection-finding question or cut from routine sends, then per-message SMS fees drop because the store stops paying to text people who show every sign of never converting.

signal.check: The SMS list has never been reviewed for subscribers with long tenure and zero orders, and campaign sends go to the full list regardless of tenure or purchase history.

risk.note: Subscribers can be re-added to full sends if they respond or order.

prerequisites: Subscriber join date and full order history on the SMS platform
steps: Build a segment: joined 1 year or more ago AND placed order 0 times over all time.
Size the segment and estimate its monthly send cost.
Send that segment a direct objection-finding question instead of the routine campaign for 1 cycle.
Move non-responders in that segment to a reduced-frequency or excluded list.
Recheck the segment's size and cost quarterly.

test.method: Not a split test; a cost and response review repeated quarterly.
test.measure: other:sms_cost_per_order before and after the review

title: Gate a bonus behind a reply-yes step in the welcome email
hypothesis: If the welcome email promises an extra bonus that is delivered only after the subscriber replies yes, then inbox placement improves and engagement rises because a reply is a strong signal to inbox providers and it trains the relationship as 2-way from the first message, on top of whatever discount code the popup already promised.
does_not_apply_when: The brand cannot reliably detect and act on a reply, such as auto-sending the bonus or routing it to a person

signal.check: The welcome flow only delivers the promised discount and never asks for or rewards a reply, even though the platform could detect and act on one.

risk.note: Gating a discount code behind a reply would add friction to the first purchase; gate only an extra, optional bonus, not the main offer.

prerequisites: A way to detect a reply and trigger delivery of the bonus, manually or automatically
steps: Pick a genuine extra bonus beyond the popup's main discount, such as a guide or checklist.
In 1 welcome email, describe the bonus with enough specifics to make it worth wanting.
Ask the subscriber to reply yes to receive it.
Set up a manual or automated process to deliver the bonus on reply within a stated time.
Track reply volume and whether replying correlates with higher opens on later sends.

test.method: Compare reply-gated welcome email against a standard welcome email with no reply step.
test.read_point: After enough new subscribers pass through the welcome flow to compare

title: Keep one fixed format for a recurring value newsletter
hypothesis: If a recurring value-first newsletter keeps the same fixed skeleton every send, such as a fixed subject prefix, 1 reward at the top, 1 tactic or story, then a CTA, then subscribers open more of it out of habit because they know what they will get, the same reason a recognisable format works for any recurring show.
does_not_apply_when: The send is a one-off promotional or launch campaign, not a recurring value newsletter

signal.check: A recurring newsletter changes its structure, length and subject style every send, with no fixed skeleton readers can learn to expect.

risk.note: A fixed format can feel stale if never refreshed; revisit periodically.

prerequisites: A recurring newsletter slot separate from promotional campaigns
steps: Define a fixed skeleton: subject prefix, top reward, 1 tactic or story, a contextual close, and a P.S.
Use the same skeleton for every send in the series for at least several cycles.
Resist changing the structure send to send, only the content inside it.
Track open and click rate trend over the series.
Only change the skeleton after a deliberate, tracked test, not on a whim.

test.method: Track open and click rate trend across a series of sends using the same fixed skeleton.
test.read_point: After 5 to 10 sends of the fixed format

title: Remove money words from value-first newsletter body copy
hypothesis: If a value-first, mostly non-promotional send removes financial or money-related words from its body copy, then inbox placement improves because inbox filters read heavy money language as a promotional signal even when the email is not actually selling.
does_not_apply_when: The email is a promotional or product send that must state a price or offer

signal.check: Value or educational sends still use money-related words and phrasing throughout, and inbox placement for those sends has never been checked against a stripped-down version.

risk.note: Copy-only change; does not apply to sends that must state a price.

prerequisites: A value or educational send type separate from promotional campaigns
steps: Pick a value or educational send that carries no offer.
Edit out money-related words and phrasing from the subject and body.
Send as usual to the normal engaged segment.
Compare inbox placement or spam rate against the same send type before the edit.
Keep the edit for value sends only; promotional sends still state price and offer normally.

test.method: Before-and-after comparison of placement or spam rate for value sends after removing money words.
test.read_point: After several value sends with the edit

title: Judge a value newsletter's health as deposits versus withdrawals
hypothesis: If every send in a newsletter or lifecycle series is labelled a deposit, pure value, or a withdrawal, a real ask, and the program is judged over a rolling period on the balance of both rather than judging each email alone, then send strategy improves because a single ask lands better after several deposits than after another ask.

signal.check: Sends are reported and reviewed 1 at a time with no label for whether each was a value deposit or an ask, so a run of consecutive asks with no deposits goes unnoticed.

risk.note: Reporting and planning change only.

prerequisites: A send calendar or log that can carry a label per send
steps: Label each planned or sent campaign as a deposit or a withdrawal.
Count the ratio of deposits to withdrawals over a rolling 30-day window.
Set a working floor, such as at least 1 deposit before every withdrawal.
Review unsubscribe and complaint rate against the deposit-to-withdrawal ratio each month.
Add more deposits before the next withdrawal if the ratio has drifted too promotional.

test.method: Not a split test; a recurring planning and review label tracked against unsubscribe trend.

title: Batch-write a fixed set of emails in 1 sitting to protect quality
hypothesis: If a finite batch of newsletter or campaign emails, such as 12 or 24, is written in 1 or 2 focused sessions instead of piecemeal under a weekly deadline, then average email quality holds because the writer is not forced to publish a weak email just to hit that week's cadence.
does_not_apply_when: The email type depends on real-time news, launches or time-bound promotions that cannot be pre-written

signal.check: Emails are written 1 at a time just before each scheduled send, under deadline pressure, and at least 1 recent send was visibly weaker because of that pressure.

risk.note: Batch content can feel dated if events change; keep a few slots open for timely news.

prerequisites: A content type that does not depend on real-time events
steps: Pick a finite batch size, such as 12 emails for a monthly send or 24 for twice-monthly.
Block 1 or 2 sessions to write the whole batch with no other task competing.
Queue the batch into the send calendar, leaving a few slots open for timely news.
Ship the batch on schedule even if a later real-time item needs to be inserted.
Compare average click rate for batch-written sends against previously rushed, one-at-a-time sends.

test.method: Compare average click rate for batch-written sends against prior one-at-a-time sends.
test.measure: email_click_rate average across the batch versus the prior period
test.read_point: After the batch has fully sent

title: Restart a dormant sending program at a low cadence
hypothesis: If a list that has not been mailed in 6 months or more restarts at once a month instead of jumping straight back to a normal cadence, and a one-time unsubscribe spike on the first send is expected and judged against list growth rather than treated as a failure, then the program recovers without the operator panicking and stopping again after the first send.

signal.check: A list has gone 6 months or more without a send, and there is no plan for how to restart, or the plan is to resume at the prior normal cadence immediately.

expected_effect.size: one-time spike expected on the first send back, then settling lower

risk.note: Cadence can be raised or lowered again based on the result.

prerequisites: A list that has gone 6 months or more without a regular send
steps: Confirm the list has been dormant for 6 months or more.
Send 1 email to restart, expecting a higher-than-normal unsubscribe rate on this first send.
Compare that unsubscribe count against new subscriber growth over the same period.
Continue at once a month while the program stabilises.
Raise frequency only while quality and unsubscribe trend both hold.

test.method: Not a split test; a restart protocol judged by unsubscribes versus list growth.
test.measure: other:unsubscribe_rate versus other:list_growth_rate after the restart send
test.read_point: Immediately after the first restart send, then monthly

title: Ask testimonial-givers for their worst moment, not their story
hypothesis: If a testimonial or review request asks the customer for the worst moment before they found the product, instead of a general how was life before question, then the resulting quotes give sharper, more specific hooks for objection-led proof emails because a worst-moment answer surfaces a concrete detail instead of a vague, generic story.

signal.check: Review or testimonial requests ask an open, general question and mostly return vague praise with no specific, quotable moment to build proof copy around.

risk.note: Copy-only change to the request question.

prerequisites: A review, testimonial or post-purchase survey step that can carry a custom question
steps: Add or change 1 question in the review or testimonial request: what was your worst moment before you found this.
Collect responses for several weeks alongside the normal review flow.
Pull out specific, concrete answers as candidate quotes.
Tag each usable quote by the objection or pain it answers.
Feed the sharpest quotes into welcome, abandonment and campaign proof emails.

test.method: Not a split test; compare the usable-quote rate from the new question against the prior general question.
test.measure: Share of responses that yield a specific, quotable hook
test.read_point: After several weeks of the new question running

title: Build an us-vs-them block with bold checkmarks and unbold X marks
hypothesis: If an us-vs-them comparison block bolds only the brand's own points with a checkmark icon and leaves competitor points unbolded with an X icon, then the visual bias toward the brand reads faster than a plain 2-column table because the reader's eye is drawn to the bolded, checked side before reading any words.

signal.check: The email design includes a competitor comparison but formats both columns identically, with no visual weight difference between the brand's points and the competitor's.

risk.note: Every comparison claim named must be substantiated; never name a competitor company directly without proof.

prerequisites: A substantiated, honest list of points that differ from the general market or a named category
steps: Write 1 strong claim as the block's sub-headline.
List the brand's points in 1 column, bolded, each with a checkmark icon.
List the comparison points in the other column, not bolded, each with an X icon.
Box each column with a light border so the contrast reads even without close reading.
Check every point named is true and provable before shipping.

test.method: A/B test the bold-and-icon comparison block against a plain, evenly formatted comparison table.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart for the email containing the block
test.read_point: After the account's normal test-size rule is met

title: Blend section backgrounds so the email scroll feels seamless
hypothesis: If section backgrounds flow into each other through matched colours or a gradient instead of showing a hard-edged, blocky seam, then fewer readers drop off partway down the email because a visibly blocky, segmented layout reads as the end of a section, inviting the reader to stop scrolling.

signal.check: Scrolling through a recent email shows a visible hard colour seam between sections instead of a matched or gradient-blended background.

risk.note: Design-only change.

prerequisites: A design tool that supports layered rectangles or gradient fills
steps: Scroll the current email top to bottom and mark any visible hard seam between sections.
Sample the dominant colour from the section above and below each seam.
Add a gradient rectangle blending the 2 colours across the seam, or set both sections to the same background colour.
Keep text and buttons layered above the background so nothing gets obscured.
Re-check on both desktop and mobile preview before sending.

test.method: Not a split test in itself; can be run as an A/B design test against the prior blocky layout.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart for the redesigned email versus the prior blocky version
test.read_point: After the redesigned version has sent enough volume to compare

title: Reverse-engineer a strong reference email's structure with AI
hypothesis: If a strong reference email is fed to an AI with a prompt chain that transcribes it, extracts a reusable structural template, then rewrites it for the brand, then new emails get written faster because the writer starts from a proven skeleton, never the source's actual words, logos or claims.
