does_not_apply_when: The result would copy a competitor's actual copy, logo, product or claims rather than only its structure

signal.check: Every new email angle is written from a blank page with no structural template to start from, even when a strong reference email exists to learn the skeleton from.

risk.note: Never copy a competitor's actual wording, logo, product or faces; extract structure only, and verify every claim before it ships.

prerequisites: An AI text tool
A strong reference email to learn from
steps: Pick a well-written reference email, the brand's own past winner or a competitor's for layout only.
Ask the AI to transcribe the email's copy.
Ask it to analyse the copy and produce a reusable structural template.
Give the brand's own details, angle and positioning, and ask it to rewrite the template for the brand.
Edit the output by hand, verifying every claim and removing any wording that echoes the source too closely.

test.method: Not a split test; track time to draft against the brand's normal copywriting process.
test.measure: other:copy_time_per_email using the structure-extraction method versus writing from scratch
test.read_point: After using the method on a few emails

title: Diagnose an underperforming email by copy, structure or design layer
hypothesis: If an underperforming email is diagnosed by where in the funnel it fails, readers never reach the offer points to a structure problem, readers reach it but do not click points to a copy or offer problem, and clicks convert poorly with a cheap or off-brand feel points to a design problem, then fixes target the actual cause instead of a generic rewrite or redesign.

signal.check: An underperforming email gets a full rewrite or redesign with no check of which specific layer, copy, structure or design, the drop-off actually happens at.

expected_effect.size: diagnostic accuracy, not a direct revenue claim

risk.note: Diagnostic method, not a live change.

prerequisites: Click-by-link or scroll-depth reporting where available
steps: Check whether readers reach the offer or CTA at all, using click-by-position or scroll data if available.
If few readers reach it, suspect structure: button placement, section order, length.
If readers reach it but do not click, suspect copy or offer: headline, benefit clarity, offer strength.
If clicks happen but convert poorly and feedback calls the email cheap or off-brand, suspect design.
Fix only the identified layer first, then re-measure before touching the others.

test.method: Not a split test; a diagnostic method applied before any rewrite or redesign.
test.measure: other:revenue_per_recipient before and after the targeted fix
test.read_point: After the next send following the targeted fix

title: Profile top Instagram followers to sharpen audience psychographics
hypothesis: If 50 to 75 of the brand's or a close competitor's top Instagram followers are reviewed for age range, gender and recurring interests, then copy angles fit the real audience better because inferred demographic and interest patterns from real profiles beat guessing from a persona document alone.
does_not_apply_when: The brand already has strong first-party demographic data from analytics or surveys

signal.check: Copy angles are written from a guessed or years-old persona document, with no recent check of the brand's or a close competitor's actual follower profiles.

risk.note: This is inference from public profiles, not a valid statistical sample; treat findings as directional. Check platform terms before recording profile data.

prerequisites: Access to the brand's or a comparable competitor's public follower list
steps: Open the brand's, or for a new brand a close competitor's, Instagram followers list.
Review 50 to 75 profiles, prioritising ones that look like real engaged followers.
Note recurring age range signals, gender split and stated interests.
Add the pattern to the brand's research notes as a directional input, not a hard rule.
Use it to sharpen 1 or 2 new copy angles and check results against the account's existing customer data.

test.method: Not a split test; a research input checked against actual conversion by angle over time.
test.measure: cvr_overall for angles informed by the profiling versus prior angles
test.read_point: After a few campaigns using angles informed by the research

title: Classify benefits as perks or insecurity anchors, then chain the anchors
hypothesis: If every product benefit is first classified as a light perk or a deeper insecurity anchor, and each anchor benefit is chained down 2 to 3 levels to the social or identity stake underneath it, then benefit-highlight copy converts better because light perks get short icon treatment while anchor benefits get the deeper emotional copy that actually moves a reader who feels that insecurity.
does_not_apply_when: The category has no real insecurity-linked benefit and forcing one would misrepresent the product

signal.check: Every benefit gets the same shallow icon-row treatment regardless of whether it is a light perk or a benefit tied to a real insecurity that could support deeper copy.

risk.note: Any external cause named in the chain must be true and provable; never blame the customer, and keep within the brand's stated voice limits.

prerequisites: A list of the product's real benefits and mechanisms from research
steps: List every benefit the product delivers.
Mark each as a perk, light and standard, or an anchor, tied to a real insecurity.
For each anchor, write the immediate result, then what that result means socially, then the deeper identity stake.
Write anchor benefits as their own longer copy block, and group perks into a short icon row.
Check every step of the chain and any external cause named is true and provable before it ships.

test.method: A/B test an anchor-chained benefit block against a plain benefit statement for the same product.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart for the email or block containing the benefit copy
test.read_point: After the account's normal test-size rule is met

title: Write emails as a stack of named blocks with a combo per email job
hypothesis: If every email is assembled from a set of named, reusable blocks, such as banner, CTA, review, product display, benefit highlight, story, countdown, featured-on and guarantee, with a known block combo picked per email job, then production speeds up because building becomes choosing and filling known blocks, not inventing a new structure each time.

signal.check: Every email is built from a fresh, one-off structure with no shared library of named content blocks or known block combos for common email jobs.

risk.note: A block library can start to feel repetitive; keep varying imagery and copy inside each block.

prerequisites: A shared file or template system to store reusable block designs
steps: List the block types the brand actually uses: banner, CTA, review, product display, benefit highlight, content or story, countdown, featured-on, guarantee.
Write a short copy and design spec for each block type.
Define 2 or 3 standard block combos for common email jobs, such as a launch, a story send, or a review-led send.
Build and save a reusable design for each block so future emails assemble rather than start from scratch.
Track build time per campaign before and after adopting the library.

test.method: Not a split test; compare build time per campaign before and after the block library is adopted.
test.read_point: After several campaigns built from the library

title: Search the problem, not the product, to map competing solutions
hypothesis: If competitor and ad research starts from the problem the product solves, such as searching hair loss instead of the product category, then the brand can see and address the full set of alternative solutions and their known complaints, because a product-name search only shows direct category competitors and misses the incumbent solutions buyers are actually comparing against.

signal.check: Competitor research only searches the brand's own product category or exact competitors, never the underlying problem, so alternative or incumbent solutions and their complaints go unseen.

risk.note: Any side-effect or complaint claim about an incumbent solution must be checked before use in copy.

prerequisites: Access to an ad library or search tool
steps: Name the core problem the product solves in plain words.
Search that problem, not the product category, in an ad library or general search.
List every incumbent or alternative solution that shows up, including outside the brand's own category.
Read complaints or objections about each incumbent solution, cross-checked in reviews.
Position 1 new angle for the brand against a real, checked complaint about an incumbent solution.

test.method: Not a split test; a research technique feeding a new copy angle to be tested as usual.
test.measure: cvr_overall for the resulting angle against the account's other angles
test.read_point: After the resulting angle runs in a campaign or flow

title: Use text-only reviews for sensitive or stigmatised objections
hypothesis: If a review used to answer a sensitive or stigmatised objection, such as a health condition someone would not want publicly tied to their face, runs as text only with no reviewer photo, while other reviews still use photos, then trust holds because the reader gets the proof without the discomfort of seeing a real identified person next to a private topic.

signal.check: Reviews answering a sensitive or stigmatised objection are shown with a reviewer photo, the same as reviews for ordinary benefits.

risk.note: Copy and formatting choice only.

prerequisites: A pool of reviews tagged by the objection each one answers
steps: Identify any review used to answer a sensitive or stigmatised objection.
Confirm the reviewer's consent covers the use, and remove any photo for that specific review.
Keep photos for reviews answering ordinary, non-sensitive objections.
Preview the mixed review block to confirm the sensitive review does not stand out awkwardly.
Note this rule in the brand's review-usage guide for future sends.

test.method: Not a split test; a formatting rule applied whenever a sensitive-objection review is used.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart for emails using this rule
test.read_point: Ongoing, whenever a sensitive-objection review is included

title: Set a graphic-to-text email ratio in the campaign calendar
hypothesis: If the monthly campaign calendar assigns a target format, graphic or plain text, to every slot at about 3 to 4 graphic sends for every 1 text send, then the mix of educational infographics and personal founder or community notes stays deliberate because format gets planned alongside content pillar instead of being decided ad hoc per email.

signal.check: The campaign calendar assigns a content pillar to each slot but never a target format, and a count of the last month's sends shows no deliberate graphic-to-text ratio.

risk.note: Planning change only.

prerequisites: A monthly campaign calendar with a slot per planned send
steps: Count last month's sends by format, graphic versus plain text.
Set a target ratio, such as 3 to 4 graphic sends for every 1 text send, for the coming month.
Assign a format to every calendar slot alongside its content pillar.
Place text-format slots where a personal voice fits, such as founder or community sends.
Recount the actual ratio at month end and adjust the target if either format is clearly underperforming.

test.method: Not a split test; a planning ratio checked against the account's own click and revenue trend by format.
test.measure: email_click_rate by format over the following month

title: Pair a campaign's email and SMS send a fixed gap apart, same day
hypothesis: If a launch or offer campaign sends by email in the morning and the matching SMS a fixed gap later the same day, such as 5 to 6 hours, instead of the 2 channels going out on unrelated schedules, then more subscribers see the message on whichever device they are using that day because the second touch catches people the first one missed without stacking both at once.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has no SMS program or the subscriber has not given SMS consent

signal.check: Email and SMS campaigns for the same launch or offer are scheduled independently, on different days or with no planned gap, rather than as a same-day paired send.

risk.note: Scheduling change only; watch for fatigue if used on every send.

prerequisites: An SMS program alongside email with a shared campaign calendar
steps: Pick a launch or time-sensitive offer campaign to pair across channels.
Schedule the email send for its normal best time.
Schedule the matching SMS 5 to 6 hours later the same day, inside legal and quiet-hour send windows.
Keep the SMS short and reference the same offer without repeating the email word for word.
Reserve this pairing for launches and offers, not every routine send, to avoid fatigue.

test.method: Compare conversion for paired same-day sends against unpaired sends of a similar campaign type.
test.measure: other:campaign_conversion_rate for paired versus unpaired campaigns

title: Delay the first conversational text a few minutes after opt-in
hypothesis: If the first conversational SMS text after a new opt-in waits a short delay, such as 5 minutes, instead of firing the instant someone submits, then reply rate may rise because a short delay reads as a real person having just seen the signup, while an instant automated reply reads as a bot.
does_not_apply_when: The brand promises an instant code and any delay would frustrate the shopper waiting to buy

signal.check: The first conversational welcome text fires the instant someone opts in, with no test of a short delay against it.

risk.note: Delay-only change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: A conversational SMS welcome step separate from the instant discount-code delivery
steps: Confirm the discount code or other promised benefit is still delivered without delay.
Add a separate conversational message, delayed about 5 minutes, that opens with a name and a low-friction question.
Test the delay length, such as 5 versus 7 minutes, against reply rate.
Keep the delay inside any applicable quiet-hour or send-time rules.
Track reply rate and downstream purchases, not reply rate alone.

test.method: A/B test the delayed conversational message against an instant version.
test.read_point: After enough new opt-ins pass through both versions

title: Hand a conversational thread to a live person at the first reply
hypothesis: If an automated conversational text sends the opening message but the thread is handed to a live person the moment a reply arrives, with the shopper's order and product context passed along so they never repeat themselves, then conversation quality and conversion rise because the shopper gets a real answer instead of another automated line.

signal.check: Replies to conversational texts are answered by more automated messages, or sit unanswered, with no defined point at which a live person takes over and no context passed to them.

risk.note: Requires staffing and a response-time target; an unstaffed handoff is worse than no conversational program at all.

prerequisites: A staffed reply queue with a stated response-time target
A way to surface order and product context to the responding agent
steps: Define the moment a thread hands off: the first inbound reply.
Route that thread to a live support or sales queue at once.
Pass the shopper's order and product context to the agent so they do not ask the shopper to repeat it.
Set and publish a response-time target for the team.
Track time from reply to human response, and whether shoppers repeat information.

test.method: Not a split test; an operational process tracked for response time and repeat-question rate.
test.measure: csat and time from reply to human response

title: Answer long conversational questions with a voice note or short video
hypothesis: If a conversational text reply that would run long, past a short, skimmable line, is instead sent as a short voice note or video with a text alternative, then the shopper gets a clearer answer and feels more familiarity with the brand because a spoken or shown explanation lands better than a wall of text on a phone screen.
does_not_apply_when: The channel or the shopper's device does not support voice or video messages

signal.check: Long conversational answers go out as multi-part text messages with no voice note or video alternative ever tried.

risk.note: Always give a text alternative for anyone who cannot or prefers not to open audio or video.

prerequisites: A messaging channel and platform that supports voice notes or short video
steps: Identify recurring questions whose answer needs more than a short text reply.
Record a short voice note or video answering the question, showing the actual product where relevant.
Send it with a brief text summary as a fallback.
Track reply and satisfaction for these answers against the prior long-text version.
Build a small library of reusable voice or video answers for the most common questions.

test.method: Compare reply rate and satisfaction for voice or video answers against multi-part text answers to similar questions.
test.measure: other:reply_rate and csat by answer format
test.read_point: After enough of each answer type to compare

title: Use iMessage text effects for a small set of specific moments
hypothesis: If iMessage's native text effects, such as a highlight animation for an important follow-up, a hidden reveal for a lapsed lead, or a celebratory animation for a signup or win, are used only for a small, defined set of moments rather than routinely, then those specific messages stand out in the thread because the effect signals genuine occasion instead of becoming background noise from overuse.
does_not_apply_when: Most of the audience is not on iMessage-capable devices
The brand has no iMessage business messaging channel

signal.check: The brand has iMessage business messaging live but has never used its native text effects, or uses them on every message rather than a defined set of moments.

risk.note: iMessage-only; falls back to plain text on other devices.

prerequisites: An iMessage business messaging channel
A mostly iPhone audience
steps: List a small set of moments worth marking, such as a key follow-up, a re-engagement attempt with a long-lapsed lead, or celebrating a signup.
Pick 1 effect per moment type and use it consistently for that moment only.
Track reply rate for effect-carrying messages against equivalent plain messages.
Stop using an effect for a moment type if it stops outperforming the plain version.
Never use an effect in a way that misrepresents who is sending the message.

test.method: Compare reply rate for messages with a text effect against equivalent plain messages for the same moment type.
test.read_point: After enough messages of each type to compare
